Components

Every component in the standard library — its symbol, what it does, and its parameters.

Symbols are rendered from the live drawing engine, with their connection leads and their pins shown unconnected — the component as you meet it in the palette, before anything is wired to it. Parameter tables are read from the component registry, so the defaults, units and on-schematic visibility below are the as-placed values by construction rather than by transcription.

Reading the tables

The first table is the component's terminals: the nets its netlist line takes, in the order it takes them. That order is what the models themselves read — a diode's anode before its cathode, a MESFET's gate before its drain — so it is worth checking before hand-writing a .cnl line; the figure above it shows where those pins sit, not which is which.

Where a terminal has a name it carries it, and where it does not the sentence under the table says whether the order matters — most two-terminal parts may be wired either way round, and a few that look symmetric may not. Read that sentence rather than the numbers: a resistor's ends are interchangeable, an inductor's stop being interchangeable the moment a Mutual couples it to another, and a taper's two ends are its two widths.

In the parameter table below it, Name is the parameter key, as it appears in the editor and in the netlist. Default and Unit are the as-placed value. A parameter marked shown appears as a label on the schematic by default; the rest are available in the parameter editor. Units accept SI prefixes (pF, nH, GHz, kΩ).

Series RLC (SRLC)

A resistance, an inductance and a capacitance in series, as one part. R, L and C are the three values; the branch impedance is R + jωL + 1/(jωC).

This is the shape a real capacitor takes above a few hundred megahertz, which is the usual reason to place one: a ceramic capacitor's datasheet gives an ESR and an ESL, and those go straight into R and L. The part is series-resonant at 1/(2π√(LC)), where its impedance falls to R — below that frequency it behaves as a capacitor, above it as an inductor. At DC the series capacitance makes the branch an open circuit.

Its pins sit exactly where a plain R, L or C's do, so you can swap one in for another without moving any wires. Its inductance can be coupled with a Mutual, which names the SRLC instance in place of an inductor.

Parallel RLC (PRLC)

The same three values in parallel — a tank. R, L and C all sit across the same two nodes, giving an admittance of 1/R + jωC + 1/(jωL).

At the parallel resonance 1/(2π√(LC)) the reactive parts cancel and the part is purely resistive at R, which is what makes it the natural way to enter a measured resonance: R sets the peak impedance, L and C set where it sits and how sharp it is. At DC the ideal inductor shorts it out.

Pin positions and Mutual coupling work exactly as they do for the SRLC above.

Series RL (SRL)

A resistance and an inductance in series, as one part: R + jωL. A real inductor, whose winding resistance is the R — and, unlike the SRLC you would otherwise place for the same job, with no third value on the schematic that nobody meant.

There is no series capacitance, so this branch does not open at DC: at ω = 0 it is simply R, which is what the physical part measures. Its inductance can be coupled with a Mutual.

Series RC (SRC)

A resistance and a capacitance in series: R + 1/(jωC). A real capacitor entered with its ESR, or a series RC damper across a resonance. At DC the capacitance makes the branch an open circuit.

It carries no inductor, so a Mutual naming one is refused rather than coupled — the refusal says so and names the part.

Series LC (SLC)

An inductance and a capacitance in series: jωL + 1/(jωC). The lossless series trap — its impedance falls to zero at 1/(2π√(LC)), which in a shunt arm is a notch. Below the resonance it behaves as a capacitor and above it as an inductor; at DC it is an open circuit.

Its inductance can be coupled with a Mutual.

Parallel RL (PRL)

A resistance and an inductance in parallel: an admittance of 1/R + 1/(jωL). The shunt form of a lossy coil, and the usual way a damped choke is entered. At DC the ideal inductor shorts it out.

Parallel RC (PRC)

A resistance and a capacitance in parallel: an admittance of 1/R + jωC. A leaky capacitor, or the shunt RC an equivalent circuit puts across a port. At DC the capacitor is an open and the part is R.

This is the one member of the RLC family that adds no branch current to the matrix — and therefore the one a Mutual cannot name.

Parallel LC (PLC)

An inductance and a capacitance in parallel: an admittance of jωC + 1/(jωL). The lossless tank — its impedance goes to infinity at 1/(2π√(LC)). For a tank with a finite peak impedance, use a PRLC and let R set the peak. At DC the ideal inductor shorts it out.

Its inductance can be coupled with a Mutual.

Ferrite Bead (Bead)

A two-terminal linear element: Rdc in series with a parallel L / Rp / Cp tank.

A bead is not an inductor and not a series RLC. The number a data sheet gives — "600 Ω at 100 MHz" — is an impedance, and the whole point of the part is that most of it is resistive at the frequency it is quoted at. That is what makes a bead absorb rather than reflect, and why it damps a supply rail where an inductor of the same reactance would ring against the decoupling capacitance. An inductor's loss is zero and a series RLC's is a constant R; a bead's rises from nothing at DC to a maximum at its ferromagnetic resonance and falls again above it.

Each element stands for a real mechanism:

Parameter What it is
Rdc The winding's own resistance. It is what the part looks like at DC, and in a power rail it is what sets the drop.
L The low-frequency inductance — what the impedance rises along.
Rp The core loss. It caps the impedance: at the parallel resonance the reactive branches cancel and |Z| is Rdc + Rp, which is the peak a data sheet plots. Nothing else sets that peak, so a bead entered without it has no maximum at all.
Cp The parallel (inter-turn) capacitance — what takes the impedance back down above resonance. A bead is not a filter above its own resonance, and this is why.

Zero means not modelled for each of the three parallel elements, never "a short" or "a zero-ohm resistor". Rp = 0 removes the loss branch and leaves an ideal L; Cp = 0 removes the capacitive branch and the impedance goes on rising; L = 0 leaves a plain Rdc.

At DC the bead is Rdc and nothing else, because the inductive branch shorts the tank out. That is both the physics and what a DC operating point needs from this part — a bead in a supply rail must not open it.

Saturation is not modelled and cannot be

A bead's inductance falls with DC bias current, sometimes by most of it, and this is a linear element. The four numbers describe the part at whatever current they were measured at, which is why a bead chosen from a small-signal impedance curve can behave quite differently in the rail it was chosen for.

Nonlinear Capacitor (NonlinearC)

A capacitor whose capacitance varies with voltage, C(V), modelled as a polynomial (Taylor) series. Enter the coefficients directly, or generate them from a C–V curve with the C–V Editor. C0 is the constant term; C1, C2, … are the higher-order coefficients, added in the editor or generated by the C–V Editor. Full treatment: The Nonlinear Capacitor & the C–V Editor.

NetTerminal
11
22

The nets of an instance line, in this order. C(V) is evaluated at V(terminal 1) − V(terminal 2), so any odd coefficient (C1, C3, …) makes the two terminals distinct. With C0 alone the capacitor is linear and they are interchangeable.

Mutual Inductance (M)

Couples two existing inductors — named by instance — with a mutual inductance, the basis for transformers and coupled resonators. It has no pins of its own; Inductor1 and Inductor2 are the instance names of the two coupled inductors and M is the mutual inductance between them.

Either name may be any part that carries an inductor: an L, an SRLC, a PRLC, an SRL, an SLC, a PRL or a PLC — every one of them holds its inductor current on a branch the coupling can act on, and every one spells its value L. Naming anything else — an SRC or a PRC included, since neither has an inductor — is reported as an error when the design is elaborated.

No terminals — this component connects to nothing on the canvas.

Ideal Transformer (Transformer)

A lossless transformer with turns ratio N:1, primary to secondary:

V(p+) − V(p−) = N · (V(s+) − V(s−)), and the secondary current is N times the primary's, flowing the other way.

Four pins on the corners — the primary p+, p− on the left, the secondary s+, s− on the right — with the dots on p+ and s+: a voltage rising at one dotted end rises at the other. Seen from the primary, a load on the secondary looks N² times larger, so N=2 between 50 Ω ports matches a 200 Ω source to a 50 Ω load.

Being ideal, it has no winding inductance and no leakage: it passes DC as readily as RF, at every frequency, harmonic balance included. For a transformer whose windings have inductance — one that blocks DC and rolls off at low frequency — use two inductors and a Mutual.

Matching Network (Match)

A synthesised bandpass matching network placed as a single two-pin component, ground being the common return. Its whole design rides in a hidden Design parameter, so what it stamps is a property of the design rather than of the component type: the ladder it contains is the synthesised one minus whatever the two external terminations already supply, since absorbing those reactances is the point. Edit it in the Match Designer.

In a netlist written by hand, leave Design out and the line's own parameters are the specification, both ends resistive: F1…F6 (with units: a bare number is hertz), Bands (1, 2 or 3), Order (match points per band), Response (ChebyshevFano, ChebyshevTwoEnded, Butterworth, Bessel), Form (Bandpass, Lowpass, Highpass), R1 and R2. A ratio the basis ladder cannot reach gets the Norton transforms, of those the Designer lists, whose values span the least. circuitrf netlist --flatten writes the ladder out as its L and C parts. A dual-band filter between 50 Ω ports:

Match:M1 in out Bands=2 F1=1.805 GHz F2=1.88 GHz F3=2.62 GHz F4=2.69 GHz Order=2 R1=50 Ohm R2=50 Ohm

A reactive termination needs Design, the Designer's JSON, which a netlist may carry as it is.

Match has its own chapter

The synthesis, the Designer's four panes, the Norton-transform rack, the Probe button and a worked two-stage interstage example are all in The Match Component. Read that before placing one — this entry is only the component's parameter table.

Tone Source (VTone)

A single-tone (sinusoidal) voltage source for harmonic balance, with an optional DC offset. V is the tone amplitude, Freq the tone frequency, and Vdc a DC offset.

In a transient analysis three more keys shape the tone, and every other analysis ignores them:

  • Delay — the tone starts at this time (seconds), and its phase is counted from it.
  • Ramp — the tone rises to full amplitude over this time along a raised cosine; 0 (the default) is a step.
  • Damping — the tone decays as e−Damping·(t − Delay) after Delay (1/s).

The DC offset is not delayed. The same three keys work on ITone, P1Tone and PnTone. A P1Tone or PnTone keeps its available power and source impedance in a transient run, and its harmonic terminations Z[k] too: the run presents each band's impedance at that band's harmonic, and its note gives the realization's error.

Current Tone Source (ITone)

The current-source dual of VTone — a single-tone sinusoidal current source with an optional DC offset. I is the tone amplitude, Freq the tone frequency, and Idc a DC offset. Use it to drive a node with a known current rather than a known voltage: an ideal current source has infinite output impedance, so it sets the current through a branch and lets the network decide the voltage.

The arrow says which way the current goes. A positive I delivers current into pin 1 (the arrowhead end, the top pin as drawn) and draws it out of pin 2. Note this is the opposite of the SPICE I element, which sinks current from its first node; circuitRF uses one direction convention for every source it has, and the glyph states it so you never have to remember which.

Like VTone, the + button in the parameter editor turns it into a multi-tone source: the scalar I/Freq migrate to I[1]/Freq[1] and each further tone gets its own Freq[n], I[n] and Phase[n].

An ideal current source is an open circuit

It contributes no conductance at all, and none whatsoever at frequencies it is not exciting. A node driven only by a current source therefore has no DC path to ground and the matrix is singular — that is the physics of the element, not a defect. Give the node a resistor, a termination or a bias path and it solves.

RF Power Source (P1Tone)

An RF source specified by available power with an internal source impedance — the natural drive for power-amplifier and loadpull work. It can also serve as an S-parameter port (via Num), and accepts per-harmonic source terminations Z[k] for harmonic source-pull.

  • Num — S-parameter port index, sharing one pool with Term.
  • Pavl — available power.
  • Z — fundamental source impedance; Freq — fundamental frequency; Phase — phase.
  • Z[k] — per-harmonic source termination: Z[0] is baseband/DC, Z[2] the second harmonic, and so on. Added in the parameter editor.

Multi-Tone RF Power Source (PnTone)

The multi-tone sibling of P1Tone — an available-power RF source that injects several carriers at once from a single component, the natural drive for two-tone intermodulation work. A freshly placed PnTone is already a two-tone source (tones 1 and 2, at 1.99 and 2.01 GHz); the + and − buttons in the editor add and remove tones. Each tone has its own Freq[i], Pavl[i] and Phase[i]; all tones share one source impedance Z and the same per-band terminations Z[k], where each mixing product is terminated by the band its frequency falls in.

Unlike P1Tone, PnTone is not an S-parameter port — it has no Num. The tones a PnTone drives must match the tones declared on the Harmonic Balance analysis: the analysis owns the mixing grid, and the source just supplies power at those frequencies.

Modulated RF Source (MOD_Source)

A modulated RF source — LTE, NR, CW, a pulsed-CW train, FSK (wireless M-Bus, Bluetooth LE), DBPSK (Sigfox), chirp spread spectrum (LoRa), a single PSK, QAM or APSK carrier or an imported I/Q waveform — for the Envelope analysis: ACLR/ACPR, EVM-style error, CCDF, AM-AM/AM-PM and two-carrier intermodulation with real signals rather than tones. One MOD_Source holds any number of carriers around its centre frequency Fc; Pavg is the total average available power behind the source impedance Z.

  • Carrier[i] — one carrier, written as a description string, e.g. "NR;BW=20MHz;SCS=30kHz;Mod=64QAM;Off=-200MHz;P=0;Seed=1": the standard (LTE, NR, CW, FILE), channel bandwidth, NR subcarrier spacing, modulation, offset from Fc, relative power (dB) and the random-data seed. BW, SCS and Off take Hz, kHz, MHz or GHz; a bare number is in Hz. A FILE carrier plays a two-column I/Q text file, File= its path and Fs= its sample rate (taken from the file's # sample_rate_hz header when absent). A PCW carrier is a pulse train, "PCW;PRI=100us;PW=50us;Rise=0.5us;Fall=0.5us;Delay=10us;Off=0;P=0": the pulse repetition interval, the width (50 % to 50 %), the 10–90 % edge times and the off-time before the rising edge (centred in the PRI when absent). Its time fields take s, ms, us (or µs) or ns; a bare number is in seconds. A PCW carrier must be the source's only carrier, and Pavg is then the pulse-top power, not the record average: see Pulsed CW. An FSK carrier is binary continuous-phase FSK, "FSK;Rb=100kbps;Dev=45kHz;BT=0.5;Data=PN9;Off=0;P=0": the bit rate (bps, kbps or Mbps), the peak deviation, the Gaussian filter's BT (absent: no filter) and the data — PN9, PN15 or a fixed pattern such as 10110100, one period of which is the record. It too must be the source's only carrier: see FSK. A DBPSK carrier, "DBPSK;Rb=100bps;Data=PN9;Off=0;P=0", takes the same Rb and Data (the Sigfox uplink: DBPSK), and a CSS carrier, "CSS;SF=7;BW=125kHz;Off=0;P=0", a spreading factor and a chirp bandwidth (LoRa: CSS); each must be the source's only carrier. An SC carrier is one root-raised-cosine-shaped carrier of PSK, QAM or APSK symbols, "SC;Rs=10Msps;Mod=16APSK;RollOff=0.2;Rings=2.85;Phases=45,15;Data=PN15;Preamble=64;PilotBlock=36/1440;Off=0;P=0": the symbol rate, the modulation (BPSK, QPSK, 8PSK, 16QAM, 64QAM, 256QAM, 16APSK, 32APSK), the roll-off, APSK's ring radii and phases, the data (PN9, PN15, PN23 or a pattern), known symbols, and optionally Span= (the filter in symbols) and Symbols= (the data symbols in the record). It must be the source's only carrier, and unlike the others with a record of their own it can be clipped: see A single carrier.
  • Record — periodic record length (s), whole 0.5 ms slots. Clip — target PAPR (dB) for clip-and-filter; absent means unclipped (the natural OFDM PAPR, about 11–12 dB). Shaping — out-of-channel spectral floor (dBc), or off.

Select the source and press Design signal… in the inspector to open the Signal Designer: the carriers and presets, or a custom I/Q file of your own, with the spectrum, the CCDF and the EVM of the signal before you simulate it.

In a harmonic-balance or loadpull run a MOD_Source is a CW tone at Fc carrying Pavg — the signal's average power, or for a pulsed-CW source the pulse-top power, the steady state of a pulse that never ends; in an S-parameter run it is the passive impedance Z.

In a native transient run it plays its signal on its carrier over a window of its record, picked by RecordStart (where in the record the run starts, default 0 s) and softened by Ramp (a raised-cosine rise over that time, default 0 s). Every other analysis ignores both.

Waveform sources

Sources for a transient analysis (type=tran), one type per waveform, each in a voltage (V_) and a current (I_) form. A voltage type's waveform is the voltage at + relative to −; a current type delivers its value into +, as the arrow shows. Every value can be an expression.

In every analysis other than transient — DC, S-parameter, harmonic balance, loadpull, envelope — a waveform source is a constant: its Dc value, or, when Dc is not set, the waveform's value at t = 0. A voltage type is then a short at every frequency but DC and a current type an open, exactly as Vdc and Idc are.

Each corner of a waveform (a pulse's edges, a PWL vertex, an exponential's start) is a time the transient analysis lands a step on exactly, so an edge is never smeared across a step.

V1 until Delay, a straight rise over Rise to V2, held for Width, a straight fall over Fall back to V1, repeating every Period (blank: one pulse). A blank Width holds V2 for the rest of the run. The current form says I1 and I2.

Voltage-Controlled Switch (VSwitch)

A resistance between p and n set by the voltage between ctrl+ and ctrl−, which draw no current: Roff at and beyond Voff, Ron at and beyond Von, and in between a smooth, monotone transition — the conductance's logarithm follows a cubic, so the conductance and its slope are continuous everywhere. A Von below Voff is inverse logic.

It works in every analysis. DC, harmonic balance and envelope runs evaluate it as the nonlinear device it is (the smooth transition is what keeps a harmonic-balance spectrum finite); an S-parameter run linearises it at its bias, so a switch biased on is Ron in series.

In a transient analysis two more keys apply:

  • Hyst — hysteresis in volts. Off, the switch does not turn fully on until Hyst/2 past Von; on, it does not turn fully off until Hyst/2 past Voff. Every other analysis ignores it, with a note.
  • TransitionPoints — at least this many accepted steps across a full crossing of the transition (default 8). The step is limited while the control voltage crosses; no step is forced to land on the crossing.

Switch is a different component: the ideal SPST/SPDT system block, set by its State.

NetTerminal
1p
2n
3ctrl+
4ctrl-

The nets of an instance line, in this order. p and n are the switched pair and interchangeable; the control voltage is ctrl+ relative to ctrl−, and swapping that pair inverts the switch.

NameDefaultUnitOn schematicMeaning
Ron1ΩshownThe resistance between p and n when the switch is on.
Roff1GΩshownThe resistance between p and n when the switch is off.
Von1VshownThe control voltage at and beyond which the switch is fully on.
Voff0VshownThe control voltage at and beyond which the switch is fully off. Between the two the conductance moves smoothly; Von below Voff is inverse logic.

Voltage-Controlled Current Source (VCCS)

An ideal transconductance: the current it delivers is G times the voltage across a separate, purely-sensing control pair, optionally delayed by T.

I = G · e^(−jωT) · (V(ctrl+) − V(ctrl−))

Four terminals in two pairs — the output pair (out+ top, out− bottom) carries the current, and the control pair (ctrl+, ctrl−, on the left) senses the controlling voltage. The control pair draws no current at all, which is what makes the source ideal and what makes the device unilateral: nothing travels backwards through it. G is the transconductance, in siemens.

T is a time delay (hidden until you set it; 0 is no delay). It multiplies the gain by e^(−jωT): unit magnitude, and a phase lag that grows in proportion to frequency, so the source has a constant group delay of T. A positive T lags. DC is unaffected, since e^0 = 1. T is the only source of phase: G itself is a real number.

The arrow says which way the current goes, and it points down: a positive G and a positive control voltage draw current in at out+ and out at out−. That is the SPICE G element's own direction, and the way a small-signal transconductance is drawn in a device model — the controlled source sinks drain current from the drain node. So a VCCS across a grounded load resistor is inverting, and a 50 Ω, G = 10 mS stage measures S21 = −0.25.

Note the VCCS's arrow points the opposite way to ITone's. That is not an inconsistency to squint past: ITone is an independent source and delivers current to its arrow pin, while the VCCS is a controlled source drawn the way controlled sources are drawn. Read each symbol's own arrow.

It works in every analysis, harmonic balance included

The VCCS is a linear device, so it is stamped into the matrix at every frequency the simulator solves at: DC, S-parameters, and every retained harmonic of a harmonic-balance run, plus everything built on those (parametric sweeps, loadpull, loadpull-pursuit). In HB it lives in the linear partition alongside the resistors and lines, and each harmonic sees its own delay phase, e^(−jkω₀T). Apart from that delay, an ideal transconductance has no frequency dependence and no compression. If you need either, the device you want is an SDD, whose equations can state them. The same is true of ITone.

1out+
2out-
3ctrl+
4ctrl-

NameDefaultUnitOn schematicMeaning
G10mSshownTransconductance: the output current per volt across the control pair.

Voltage-Controlled Voltage Source (VCVS)

An ideal voltage gain: the voltage it holds across its output pair is E times the voltage across a separate, purely-sensing control pair, optionally delayed by T.

V(out+) − V(out−) = E · e^(−jωT) · (V(ctrl+) − V(ctrl−))

Four terminals in two pairs, laid out exactly as the VCCS's are — the output pair (out+ top, out− bottom) and the control pair (ctrl+, ctrl−, on the left), which draws no current at all. E is a voltage ratio and carries no unit.

T is a time delay, exactly as on the VCCS: the gain becomes E · e^(−jωT), and E itself is a real number.

The two tiles differ in one thing: what the diamond carries. The VCCS's arrow points at the current it delivers; the VCVS has a ± pair down its axis instead, because there is no current direction to point at. A VCVS states a potential difference and whatever current the rest of the circuit draws through it flows — including none, if nothing is connected across the output pair. That is the ideal source's own behaviour, not a limitation.

Being ideal, its output impedance is zero: it holds E times the control voltage no matter what it is loaded with. Put a series resistor after it if you want a source with an impedance.

It works in every analysis, harmonic balance included

Like the VCCS, the VCVS is a linear device stamped at every frequency the simulator solves at, harmonic balance included, with each harmonic seeing its own delay phase. It carries a branch-current unknown of its own where the VCCS carries none — a relation between node voltages is not something admittances can express — but nothing about that is visible from outside. For a gain that varies with frequency in any other way, or with drive or bias, the device you want is an SDD.

An ideal current source is an open circuit

The output pair gets no conductance of its own, so — exactly as with ITone — an output node with nothing else attached to it has no DC path to ground and the matrix is singular. Load it.

Operational Amplifier (OpAmp)

A triangle with the inverting input in− above the non-inverting input in+, and the output out at its point, referenced to ground.

With A=0, the default, it is ideal — infinite open-loop gain. Its inputs draw no current and are held at the same voltage, and the output delivers whatever current that takes, so the feedback network alone sets the gain: an inverting stage with Rin and Rf has a gain of exactly −Rf/Rin.

A non-zero A makes it a finite-gain amplifier, V(out) = A · (V(in+) − V(in−)), with an output resistance Rout behind it. As A grows, the answers converge on the ideal ones. Rout acts only with a finite A.

It is linear and the same at every frequency: there is no bandwidth, slew rate or output swing limit, so an op-amp left without negative feedback has an output nothing bounds. For a gain that rolls off, put the roll-off in the circuit around it.

Terminals & ports

Ground (GND)

The global reference node (net 0). No parameters.

Term

An S-parameter port: a numbered, reference-impedance termination where the simulator excites and measures. Num is the port index, auto-assigned at placement; Z is the reference impedance. See Pins, Ports & Terms for how it differs from a Pin.

Outside S-parameters a Term is a load of Z to its reference: its resistance (the real part of Z) in a DC run, and Z at every harmonic in a harmonic-balance or loadpull run. A bias or a current returning through it flows, as it would through the instrument it stands for. Put a DC block in front of a Term on a biased node, exactly as on a bench. A Term inside a cell is ignored in every analysis.

Current Probe (IProbe)

Voltage Probe (VProbe)

A one-terminal voltage probe. Drop it anywhere on a wire and that net is reported under the probe's instance name — Vout, say. That name is what the trace picker lists and what a measurement expression reads: V("Vout").

It is a label, not a part. It has one terminal, so it cannot bridge two nets; the elaborator builds no model for it, so it stamps nothing; and a design simulates identically with every VProbe deleted. Placing one can never change an answer — it can only add a name to it.

On an unnamed wire the probe's name becomes the net's name. There is one row in the results, called Vout, and no n7 beside it — the automatic name was never a name anyone chose, and two rows for one point in the circuit is one row too many.

On a wire you have already labelled, both names appear. The label is not overwritten: a wire labelled n_drain with a Vout probe on it shows up twice — as n_drain and as Vout — carrying the same voltage. The probe is an alias there, and either name plots and measures the same node.

Two rules keep the names unambiguous, and breaking either refuses the run rather than reporting:

  • Two VProbes may not share a name.
  • A VProbe may not share a name with a net.

A VProbe that touches nothing is reported in the Messages panel and drops out of the results, rather than reporting a plausible number for a point you never probed. So is one placed on ground, which is 0 V by definition.

It is the one component you can drag off a wire. Every other symbol takes its wires with it when you move it, because moving the picture must never re-wire the circuit. A probe has nothing to re-wire, so dragging it leaves the drawing exactly as it was and puts the probe wherever you dropped it — pick it up, look somewhere else, run again, with no repair work in between. Rotating it behaves the same way, and a wire dragged out from under a probe simply leaves it behind.

Select the probe and its wire together and they move as one, so the probe stays on the net.

One terminal, v — an instance line writes a single net. One terminal, at the arrow's tip. It taps the net it touches and names it after the instance; there is no second terminal to get the wrong way round, and nothing it can short together.

No parameters.

Stability Probe (WSProbe)

A stability probe, placed in a node so that it splits the node into a generator-side terminal (G) and a load-side terminal (L). It implements T. A. Winslow, General Circuit Analysis Using The WSProbe (2023); every quantity below is that document's, under its own name.

Electrically it is an IProbe — a 0 V short — and it is placed the same way: drop it onto the wire whose node you want to look at, and circuitRF deletes the stretch of wire between its two pins so the probe breaks into the run instead of being shorted by it. It perturbs nothing, so a design simulates identically with every WSProbe deleted. It takes no parameters.

The letters are the orientation. G is the generator-side terminal and L the load-side one: ZG looks out of G, ZL out of L. Rotating or mirroring the symbol moves the drawing and never the pin order, so swapping the two means swapping the wires — which swaps every G/L-labelled output and negates nothing else.

What it produces is not a number but a matrix. An S-parameter run with any WSProbe in it writes a wsp cube — 2N x 2N for N probes — and six named outputs per probe: H0 and Y0, the driving-point impedance and admittance; ZG and ZL, the bidirectional impedances; LG, the bilateral loop gain; and F = 1 - LG. Two stability margins, SM_Y0 and SM_H0, come with them. Everything else the document derives — every other loop gain, the reduced two-port at the probe, the probe-pair blocks, the global loop gains over a set of probes — is post-processing of that one matrix, and is available in the Data Display's trace card and in a measure line.

Reading a node for stability is two plots, not one. Plot 1/H0 and 1/Y0 on a polar chart and look for a clockwise crossing of the negative real axis; the trace card reports the frequencies it finds, or none. Both must be checked, because a zero can hide the pole in one of them but never in both — a series resonance shows in 1/Y0 alone and a parallel one in 1/H0 alone.

The stability margin is a distance, and the search is the detector. SM_Y0 and SM_H0 are unitless numbers in [0, 1], shown in dB (20*log10), and the trace card prints each one's minimum beside the crossing search that pairs with it. A node with positive resistance on both sides can never read below -12 dB, so anything under that line certifies negative resistance on one side; the run reports any probe whose margin falls below the analysis' MarginThreshold (default -15 dB) as worth looking at. That report is a note, not a warning: a low margin is somewhere to look, not a failure.

The WSProbe has its own chapter — every quantity with its equation, the probe pairs, the global loop gains, the stability envelope, the probe under harmonic balance, the NDF, and an appendix on stability analysis itself.

NetTerminal
1G
2L

The nets of an instance line, in this order. G is the generator-side terminal, L the load-side. ZG looks out of G, ZL out of L; swapping them swaps every G/L-labelled output and negates nothing else.

No parameters.

Oscillator Probe (OscProbe)

The marker an oscillator analysis needs: it says where in the circuit the oscillation is looked for. Place exactly one, where the oscillation is strong:

  • Mode=series (the default): in the oscillator's loop, the way an IProbe is placed. Drop it onto a wire and it breaks into the wire.
  • Mode=shunt: across the resonator, often from the tank's live side to ground.

In every other analysis it does nothing: a short in series, an open in shunt. So a design runs the same with it as without it.

Under the oscillator analysis it holds a generator at the oscillation frequency only. In shunt it is a voltage generator, and the analysis finds the amplitude and frequency at which it draws no current. In series it is a current generator, and the analysis finds where it holds no voltage. Either way the generator does no work at the answer, so the circuit is oscillating on its own. Its two terminals are interchangeable.

In depth: Simulations › Oscillator, and its phase noise.

NetTerminal
11
22

The nets of an instance line, in this order. Interchangeable. In series (Mode=series) it sits IN the oscillator's loop; across the resonator (Mode=shunt) it joins the two sides of the tank, often one of them ground.

Tuner / SourceTuner / LoadTuner

A programmable RF termination. The three variants are the same engine component with different glyphs and net ordering — match the symbol to its role. SourceTuner sits on the source side, LoadTuner on the load side.

  • Z[1] — the fundamental termination. Required, and it accepts complex literals such as 50+j*10. Add Z[2], … in the editor, or G[k] to give a reflection coefficient instead.
  • Zdefault — the catch-all termination for harmonics not otherwise specified, and the impedance the tuner presents at DC.
  • Z0 — the reference impedance for any G[k] entry.
  • BiasTee — on or off, chosen from a picker. on builds the internal bias-tee and DC supply, which the loadpull directive requires. With it off the tuner is RF-only: there is no DC path through it to the reference node.
  • Vbias — the DC bias at the DUT-facing port when the bias-tee is on.
  • ShowBias — true or false, chosen from a picker. Display only: it draws the bias-tee on the glyph and never reaches the engine, so the extracted netlist is identical either way.

One terminal, 1 — an instance line writes a single net.

Which analyses a tuner works in

All five that terminate a circuit: DC, S-parameters, harmonic balance, loadpull and loadpull pursuit. It is an ordinary linear component, so a parametric sweep wrapping any of them sweeps it like anything else.

How its frequency response is defined

A tuner is not a fitted network. It presents the impedance you declared, exactly, with no interpolation between entries and no roll-off. Which entry it presents depends on the analysis:

Analysis What the tuner presents
DC Zdefault — but behind the ideal DC-block capacitor, so with BiasTee=on the DC seen at the pin is the supply through the choke, and with BiasTee=off the pin is open at DC.
S-parameters Z[1], flat across the whole frequency sweep. There is no harmonic structure outside harmonic balance, so the declared fundamental is the only value in play — Z[2], Z[3], … are ignored.
Harmonic balance Z[k] at harmonic k, where k is the analysis fundamental's k-th multiple. Anything not declared falls back to Zdefault, as does any frequency that is not on the harmonic grid.
Loadpull / pursuit The same per-harmonic rule, except that the harmonic being tuned takes its value from the grid point under test rather than from Z[k].

So the answer to "what does Z[2] do in an S-parameter run?" is nothing: declare the band you care about in Z[1], and use several S-parameter analyses if you want several terminations.

In loadpull and pursuit, the SourceTuner is also the RF generator

A loadpull run needs a drive as well as terminations, and the SourceTuner supplies it: the loadpull and pursuit engines assign it the source role, which stamps a single-tone RF generator inside it, behind the impedance it presents. The generator is calibrated to available power — |Vs| = √(8·Pavl·Re Z1) — so the power you ask for and the impedance the DUT is driven from stay consistent as either one moves across the sweep.

The drive level is not a tuner parameter. There is no Pavl row on the component, because the sweep over drive belongs to the run, not to the part. The ladder is set in the analysis: Pin start (dBm), Pin max (dBm) and Pin step (dB) in the Loadpull and Loadpull Pursuit setup, walked upward from the start until compression is reached or the cap stops it.

Outside loadpull, a SourceTuner does not drive

The source role is assigned by the loadpull and pursuit engines only. Place a SourceTuner on a plain harmonic-balance testbench and it behaves as a passive termination like the other two glyphs — put a P1Tone or a tone source on the bench for the drive.

Transmission lines

Ideal Transmission Line (TLIN)

An ideal transmission line of characteristic impedance Z, stated one of two ways:

  • Electrical (the default): electrical length E at a reference frequency F. Optional loss A is the total in dB at F, scaling in proportion to frequency.
  • Physical: length L with effective permittivity Eeff (default 1, an air line), so the electrical length is θ(f) = 2π·f·L·√Eeff / c₀ with no reference frequency needed. Loss is per unit length: Ac (conductor, scaling as √f) and Ad (dielectric, scaling as f), both in dB/m at F and both 0 by default.

A line states E or L, never both; Eeff below 1, A together with L, and Ac or Ad without F are refused. In the parameters dialog, Use physical length / Use electrical length switches form, converting at F (or at 1 GHz when there is none) so the line does not change; the new L is written in the technology's length unit. For a physical-form line, circuitrf explain reports the electrical length it resolves to at F.

TLIN:TL1 a b Z=50 Ohm L=25 mm Eeff=3.2 Ac=4 Ad=2 F=2 GHz

Loss and phase. A line's loss comes with the phase a physical loss has, in every analysis. The conductor term (Ac) adds an internal reactance equal to its loss. The dielectric term (A or Ad) makes the line slightly slower below F and slightly faster above it, as a material with a flat loss tangent is. At F the line is exactly as stated.

In a transient analysis a lossless line is exact: each end sees Z in series with the wave that left the other end one delay earlier, and an edge crossing the line lands on a step. A lossy line runs as that delay plus a rational fit of the rest of its response. The run's note gives the fit's departure from the line up to the run's highest frequency (half the inverse of the largest step). A line that cannot be fitted within 10⁻³ there is refused by name, with its error.

The angle form's loss is A, total dB at F, ∝ f; the physical form's is Ac (conductor, ∝ √f) and Ad (dielectric, ∝ f), both dB/m at F, both default 0. A with L is refused.

Coupled Line (CLIN)

An ideal, lossless pair of coupled transmission lines over a common ground, specified by its even-mode impedance Ze, odd-mode impedance Zo and electrical length E at a reference frequency F. Like TLIN it has no substrate and no layout; it is the four-port to reach for when designing a coupler or a coupled-line filter section before committing to a geometry.

  • Match. All four ports are matched to Z0 when Ze · Zo = Z0²; the default 69.37 Ω / 36.04 Ω pair is matched to 50 Ω.
  • Coupling. At a quarter wave (E = 90° at F) the coupled-port voltage is (Ze − Zo) / (Ze + Zo) — about −10 dB for the defaults.
  • Inhomogeneous media. Eo is the odd mode's electrical length. Left blank, both modes share E, which is the homogeneous (stripline) case with ideal isolation. Set it shorter than E to model a medium such as microstrip, where the odd mode travels faster and the directivity is finite.

In a transient analysis the pair runs exactly, as its even and odd modes, each a delay of its own. The physical coupled lines (MCLIN, BCLIN, MBCLIN) have loss and dispersion and are refused there by name.

NameDefaultUnitOn schematicMeaning
Ze69.37ΩshownEven-mode characteristic impedance, in ohms: what each line looks like when both are driven in phase. Never below Zo. The pair is matched to Z0 when Ze x Zo = Z0 squared.
Zo36.04ΩshownOdd-mode characteristic impedance, in ohms: what each line looks like when the two are driven in antiphase. At a quarter wave the coupling is (Ze - Zo) / (Ze + Zo).
E90degshownElectrical length at F, in degrees — the even mode's, and the odd mode's too unless Eo is set. 90 is a quarter wave, where the coupling peaks.
F1GHzshownThe frequency E (and Eo) are quoted at. Both scale in proportion to frequency.
Eo—deg—Odd-mode electrical length at F, in degrees. Leave it blank for a homogeneous medium (stripline), where both modes travel together; set it to model an inhomogeneous one such as microstrip, where the odd mode is faster and so electrically shorter.

Broadside-Coupled Stripline (BCLIN)

A pair of strips on two adjacent conductor layers, one above the other, between two ground planes in one dielectric — the offset broadside-coupled stripline used for tight (3 dB and closer) couplers. Its pins are CLIN's: 1 and 2 are strip A (the upper one), 3 and 4 strip B, with 3 beside 1.

  • Geometry. W is the strip width (both strips), O the lateral offset between their centres (0 puts one directly over the other) and L the length. The cross-section — Hs between the strips' facing surfaces, Ha from strip A up to its ground, Hb from strip B down to its ground, the thickness T and Er — starts empty, which means from the stackup: LayerA (default: the first signal conductor with another signal conductor directly beneath it and a ground plane above and below) and LayerB (the next conductor down) are resolved on the technology, every layer between two surfaces counting toward their spacing. Typing a value into one of those rows overrides the stackup for that row only; with no technology the run says which rows take their standalone defaults.
  • Physics. The cross-section is solved by circuitRF's own 2D quasi-static field solver (finite differences on a graded grid, thick strips, the two grounds), once per geometry. Both modes travel at c/√εr; the even- and odd-mode impedances follow from the capacitance matrix. An asymmetric stack (Ha ≠ Hb, unequal thicknesses) is described by the symmetric average of the two strips, and the run says so when they differ by more than 5 %.
  • Loss. Conductor loss is integrated over the solved surface-charge distribution (both strips and both grounds), dielectric loss is exact for the homogeneous medium.

Microstrip Line (MLIN)

A physical microstrip line on the current technology's substrate: W is the conductor width and L the length. Unlike TLIN, its impedance and loss follow from the geometry and the substrate rather than being stated. The parameters dialog shows the Z0 (and εeff) the current W gives on the resolved substrate; type a Z0 there instead and W is set to the width that gives it, as one undoable edit.

The length can be stated electrically instead, as E at F in place of L, exactly as a TLIN's is: Use electrical length in the parameters dialog converts the current L at the line's own εeff, and Use physical length converts it back, so switching never changes the line a run simulates. CPWG and SLIN have the same button. Layout always draws the physical length.

Loss and phase. The substrate's Er and TanD are the values at 1 GHz. A loss tangent that stays the same over many decades comes with a permittivity that falls slowly as frequency rises, so MLIN, CPWG and SLIN lines are slightly slower below 1 GHz and slightly faster above it. A long line on a lossy board, such as 25 mm on FR4 with TanD 0.02, gains about 7° less phase at 10 GHz than a constant Er would give. The conductor loss also brings the metal's internal inductance, which adds a little phase. Neither changes the Z0 or εeff the dialog reports. In a transient analysis these lines run as a delay plus a rational fit, as a lossy TLIN does.

Grounded Coplanar Waveguide (CPWG)

A coplanar waveguide over a ground plane: a strip of width W with ground copper on the same layer a gap G from each edge, and a plane under the substrate. The substrate and the backing plane come from the technology, as an MLIN's do; the gap is the line's own. When the coplanar ground is far from the strip the line is a microstrip, and CPWG gives the same answer an MLIN would. The parameters dialog shows the Z0 and εeff at the top frequency of the schematic's S-parameter sweep, and a Z0 typed there sets W. Against a 2-D field solve its Z0 is within about 2 % over the gaps and widths PCB and MMIC lines use. Update Layout from Schematic draws the strip, and a ground strip as wide as the strip on each side of it; the vias that tie those grounds to the plane are yours to add.

Stripline (SLIN)

A strip of width W buried between two ground planes, centred or offset. The planes are the nearest ground-designated conductors above and below SignalLayer, and the dielectric between them sets the two heights, εr and the loss — when that dielectric is several layers of different εr, the line uses their thickness-weighted mean and says so. Update Layout from Schematic draws the strip on SignalLayer.

Swapping one line type for another

Right-click a TLIN, MLIN, CPWG or SLIN and choose Swap Line Type to turn it into one of the others in place, or choose the type from the type field at the top of its parameters dialog. With several lines selected, the context menu swaps all of them as one undo step; a line that cannot be swapped is named in Messages and the rest still swap.

The instance name, its wiring and its position stay the same, and so do W and L — the impedance follows from the new line type, and the parameters dialog shows it.

  • To CPWG, the gap is the one measured off the artwork when the line came from Create Schematic from Artwork; otherwise the line's earlier G, if it had one; otherwise you are asked for it.
  • To TLIN, Z and Eeff are what the old line has at the top frequency of the schematic's S-parameter sweep, with its loss as Ac and Ad; the TLIN is in its physical form.
  • From TLIN, W is the line's earlier width when it had one, and otherwise the width that gives Z at that frequency (Messages says when it was worked out this way). An electrical-form TLIN's E becomes a length.
  • To SLIN, the signal layer needs a plane above and below it; on any other layer the swap is refused and the line is left as it was.

Nothing is lost: a parameter the new type does not have (CPWG's G, a TLIN's Z, a layer choice) is kept with the component, so swapping straight back gives the original line exactly. Each type takes its substrate from the technology. An MBEND, MTEE, MCROSS or MTAPER next to a swapped line stays a microstrip discontinuity, and Messages says so.

Coupled Microstrip Lines (MCLIN)

A symmetric pair of edge-coupled microstrip lines on the technology's substrate: strip width W, edge-to-edge gap S and length L. Its pins are CLIN's (1/2 line A, 3/4 line B, 3 beside 1), so a CLIN in a schematic can be replaced by one without rewiring.

The even- and odd-mode impedances and effective permittivities come from the Kirschning–Jansen coupled-microstrip equations, with their frequency dispersion and a correction for the strips' thickness; the two modes keep their own εeff, so the odd mode is faster and the isolation of a coupler is finite, as on a real board. Conductor, roughness and dielectric loss are MLIN's, per mode. The published range is W/h and S/h from 0.1 to 10 and εr up to 18; outside it the result is still computed and the run says it is an extrapolation. On placement W starts at the workspace's 50 Ω width and S at the same value.

N Coupled Microstrip Lines (MCLINN)

N edge-coupled microstrip strips on the technology's substrate, all of length L. Every strip is W wide and every gap S unless it states its own: add a row W[k] for strip k (strip 1 is the top one) or S[k] for the gap below it. Terminals 1 to N are the strips' near ends and N + 1 to 2N their far ends, so strip k runs from k to N + k, and the symbol grows with N. Two strips are MCLIN's pair with its pins in that order, not CLIN's.

Every strip couples to every other. A strip in an interdigital or combline filter couples to both neighbours at once and, more weakly, to the strips beyond them, which no chain of coupled pairs can describe. circuitRF solves the cross-section itself: its 2D field solver gives the strips' capacitance matrix with the substrate and without it, the second gives the inductance matrix (L = μ₀ε₀·C₀⁻¹), and the line's N modes are the eigenvectors of L·C, each with its own impedance and its own εeff. The terminal network is those modes recombined, the multiconductor-line method of Tripathi and Lee, in the modal form of Paul's book. Conductor and roughness loss are MLIN's per strip, dielectric loss its filling-factor form.

Its limits. The solve is quasi-static, done once per geometry: there is no dispersion, so each mode keeps its static εeff and impedance at every frequency, and past a cross-section a tenth of a wavelength across the run says so. The solver is within about 0.5 % for strips with thickness; strips with T = 0 come out up to about 1.2 % low in impedance, and the run says that too. Against MCLIN on 20 mil RO4350B at 1 GHz, two 1.1 mm strips 0.2 mm apart have their even and odd impedances within 1.2 % and their S-parameters within 0.008. On placement W starts at the workspace's 50 Ω width and S at the same value, as MCLIN's.

Broadside-Coupled Microstrip (MBCLIN)

BCLIN's broadside pair without the upper ground: strip B is buried in the dielectric Hb above the ground plane, strip A sits Hs above it — on the top surface by default (Hd empty), or buried too when Hd or the stackup puts dielectric over it — and there is air above. Its pins are CLIN's.

Because the medium is not uniform, the field solver runs twice — with the dielectric and with air — and each mode gets its own impedance and its own εeff; as with MCLIN the modes travel at different speeds, which limits the directivity. The two strips are never symmetric here (they sit at different heights), so the pair is always described by the symmetric average of the two, and the run says how far apart they are. The cross-section rows and LayerA/LayerB follow the stackup exactly as BCLIN's do, with the one ground plane below strip B.

Microstrip Curve (MCURVE)

A radiused (curved) microstrip bend: width W, turn Angle (counter-clockwise positive, as MBEND's) and Radius, the centre-line radius. Where MBEND is a corner with a discontinuity, a curve has no corner — it is modelled as the line it nearly is, an MLIN of the same width over the effective length (R − 0.2·W)·|Angle|. The electrical path is a little shorter than the drawn centre line because the current favours the inner edge.

That rule is published for Radius between 3W and 7W. Outside it the result is still computed and the run says it is an extrapolation; below 2W a bend is more than a change of length and the run tells you to EM-simulate it. A radius below W/2 cannot be drawn and is refused. The reference planes are the two ends of the arc, so an MCURVE butts straight onto an MLIN with no overlap to subtract. In layout it is drawn with true arc edges, which EM, DRC and the exporters flatten to the technology's own tolerance.

Microstrip Mitred Bend (MMITER)

A chamfered (mitred) microstrip corner: width W, turn Angle (counter-clockwise positive, as MBEND's, anywhere up to 120°) and miter M. M is the fraction of the corner's outer-to-inner diagonal that is cut away, measured from the outer corner — the Douville–James definition — so at 90° M = 0.5 runs the cut corner to corner across the W×W corner square, and larger values cut deeper. On placement M starts at the Douville–James optimum for the workspace's 50 Ω line, which is the cut that best cancels the corner's reflection on a right-angle bend; at other angles that same fraction is a reasonable starting point rather than an optimum.

Electrically the bend is the line it is drawn as — an MLIN of the corner's own centre-line length — plus a small correction for what the corner does that a straight line would not. That correction comes from a table characterised with circuitRF's own planar EM over W/h, εr, angle and miter, and is interpolated in between, so any angle and miter inside the range work, not only 45° and 90°.

The pins sit where the strip is full width again: at 90° with M up to 0.5 these are the edges of the W×W corner square (MBEND's planes); a deeper chamfer moves them out a little, and the extra line is part of the part. Draw the MLINs either side from the pins. W/h between 0.35 and 7 and εr between 2.2 and 13 are characterised; outside that the result is still computed and the run says it is an extrapolation. An angle past 120° or a miter deeper than the table covers (0.6 at 45° and below, 0.8 from 90°) is refused. Conductor thickness enters through the line part only.

Microstrip Gap (MGAP)

The end-to-end gap between two microstrip lines of the same width: W is the width of the line on each side and S the gap, edge to edge, from one line's end to the other's. Use it wherever a gap is part of the design — the coupling between the resonators of a gap-coupled filter, an end-coupled feed, or a DC break in a line — so that the gap is a value you can see, sweep and optimise rather than a distance two lines happen to be apart. The two terminals are interchangeable.

Electrically the gap is a series capacitance across it and a shunt capacitance from each line end to ground, from closed-form fits that are stated over 0.5 ≤ W/h ≤ 2, 0.1 ≤ S/W ≤ 1 and 2.5 ≤ εr ≤ 15. Outside that range the result is still computed and the run says it is an extrapolation. The capacitances do not change with frequency and carry no loss. Checked against circuitRF's own electrostatic EM solve on a 0.508 mm, εr 3.66 substrate: up to W/h = 1 the gap's |S21| is within 0.5 dB and its phase within 0.5°; at W/h = 2 the closed form reads the series capacitance 8–14 % low (|S21| up to 1.3 dB low), and at W/h = 2 with S = W — both ratios at the edge of the range — it reads it 43 % low, 4.9 dB in |S21|. Where the gap is the design, check it by EM there. S must be greater than zero: a gap of zero is two lines touching, and the simulation refuses it.

In the layout, MGAP draws no copper. Its layout is its two pins, S apart and each W wide, and the lines placed on either side are the metal — so when the layout is updated from the schematic, the two line ends land exactly S apart. Its two pins are on different nets, so LVS reads the gap as a designed break, not an open.

Microstrip T-Junction (MTEE)

A three-port microstrip T-junction. W1, W2 and W3 are the widths of the three arms, and L1, L2 and L3 their lengths from the junction's centre to each pin — the shape the layout draws.

The arms are simulated as microstrip lines, with the junction model between them. A through arm carries L1 − W3/2 (or L2 − W3/2) of line, the branch L3 − max(W1, W2)/2: the junction model starts where the crossing arm's edge is. When the branch reaches no further than the through line's edge, the tee is a straight line with pin 3 on it, and it simulates as exactly that — two lines of L1 and L2 meeting at pin 3 — so with pin 3 open it gives the same answer as an MLIN of L1 + L2. Any longer branch brings the junction model in.

A tee with no L values (from a file saved before they existed) simulates the junction alone, and the run says its arms are not simulated.

Microstrip Cross-Junction (MCROSS)

A four-port microstrip cross-junction, with a width (W1–W4) and a length from the centre (L1–L4) per arm.

The arms are simulated as microstrip lines with the junction model between them, as for the MTEE: arms 1 and 3 carry L − max(W2, W4)/2 of line, arms 2 and 4 L − max(W1, W3)/2. When arms 2 and 4 both stop at the edge of arms 1 and 3, the cross is a straight line — the lines of L1 and L3 with pins 2 and 4 on it — and with those pins open it equals an MLIN of L1 + L3. The same holds the other way round. A cross with no L values simulates the junction alone, and says so.

Radial Stub (MRADIAL)

An open stub shaped as a fan: a sector of microstrip whose narrow end is as wide as the line it hangs from (W), whose open arc is Ro from the sector's apex, and which opens through Angle. With Sides = 2 it is a butterfly, a second sector back to back with the first on the same node. Use it where an open stub has to be a short over a band: the RF ground at the end of a bias line, or a shunt stub of a low-pass or band-stop filter. Its one terminal is the shunt node, the middle of the narrow end; hang it on a tee's branch or on the end of a line. It returns through the ground plane.

How it works. Between the sector and the plane the wave spreads out from the apex as a cylindrical wave, so the stub is a line whose impedance falls as the sector widens. Open at the arc, its input impedance is the radial line's closed form, in Bessel functions of the wave across the sector. It is a short at its first resonance, and because it widens, that comes at a shorter length than a straight stub's quarter wave, with a broader null. On 20 mil RO4350B, a 60° stub with W = 1.1 mm and Ro = 8 mm shorts at 3.86 GHz, where its length past the narrow end is two thirds of a straight line's quarter wave; shunted across a 50 Ω line it holds |S21| below −20 dB from 3.64 to 4.08 GHz.

What circuitRF computes, at each frequency:

  • the radius at which the sector is as wide as its feed, r_i = W / (2·sin(Angle/2)). The copper starts there;
  • the effective permittivity: the microstrip line model's, dispersion included, for a line as wide as the sector's chord at its mean radius;
  • the effective radius: the arc moved out by that line's open-end length, the fringing past an open end;
  • conductor and dielectric loss, that line's own, carried in the wave.

A butterfly is its two sectors in parallel.

Limits. The closed form carries one radial wave. Once the arc is about a guided wavelength long, a feed at the middle excites the sector's next mode, which it does not carry; the run says so. The microstrip line model's range applies to the equivalent line and is reported for it: a very wide or very short sector is outside it. The junction where the feed meets the narrow end is not modelled, and neither is the fringing along the sector's two straight edges: the impedance level is the sector's own arc width. That moves the stub's slope near its resonance more than where the resonance falls. A butterfly's two sectors do not see each other in the model.

In the layout the stub is one outline: the narrow end on the pin, facing the feed, and the arc a true arc. A butterfly's pin is between its two sectors and faces across them, so on the end of a line its wings spread to either side of the line. Angle is in degrees, up to 180°; a Ro that does not reach past r_i is refused.

One terminal, 1 — an instance line writes a single net. One terminal, the shunt node: the middle of the sector's narrow end, where the feed line of width W meets it. The stub is open at its arc and returns through the ground plane.

NameDefaultUnitOn schematicMeaning
W2.9mmshownWidth of the feed line the stub hangs from: the sector's narrow end is this wide.
Ro29mmshownRadius of the open arc, measured from the sector's apex (behind the narrow end). About a quarter wavelength past the narrow end puts the stub's short circuit at the frequency of interest.
Angle60degshownThe sector's angle, up to 180°. Wider is a lower impedance and a broader null.
Sides1—shown1: one sector. 2: a butterfly, a second sector back to back with the first on the same node, two stubs in parallel.

Drawn Metal (MSHAPE)

Copper you draw: a pad, a launch, a flag, any shape no line model covers. With Form = "polygon" it is the closed outline through its corners; with Form = "path" it is a centreline of width W through them. The corners are the rows X[1], Y[1], X[2], Y[2], … and the pins the rows PinX[k], PinY[k], PinW[k] (the pin's width) and PinDir[k] (the way it faces, in degrees), all in the part's own frame, the origin where the layout puts the part. Every row is an expression, so a corner can follow a parameter (X[2] = Lpad). It is placed with a 100 µm square and one pin in the middle of its left edge; + in the parameter editor adds a corner, and a pin is added as its four rows.

There is one terminal per PinX[k] row, numbered by k, and pin k is port k. In the layout the shape is drawn on SignalLayer (empty: the technology's top conductor) with a pin of PinW[k] at each pin.

Model says what a circuit simulation does with it. Model = "open" leaves its terminals open, which is what a pad at the end of a line is to a first approximation. Model = "short" makes its terminals one node, an ideal junction or the star pad where several parts meet. Model = "none" gives it no circuit model at all: a schematic that holds one can only be simulated by EM, so a run by circuit models is refused naming it and an optimisation uses em=direct. Write the two words quoted in a netlist, as Form="polygon" and Model="open".

It is the drawn copper of the PCell Designer, where Stretch by Parameter ties corners to a parameter and a placed copy of the cell shows a drag handle for it. In LVS it is a conductor, as a line is.

Via (VIA)

A plated via changing layers: terminal A lands on FromLayer, B on ToLayer. Its inductance, resistance and capacitance are computed from the technology's stackup — the barrel length, the drill it belongs to, the ground planes it passes and any stub where the drill runs on — so none of them is typed. Every row may be left empty to follow the technology; the parameter dialog shows the L, R and C that result. The formulas, where they hold and how they compare with a 3D solve are in Vias.

Test Point Pad (TESTPAD)

A round test-point pad on an RF line: a pad of diameter D on PadLayer — by default the lowest signal conductor, the board's far side — fed either through a via at its centre from ViaFrom (Feed = Via) or by a short stub leaving it on one side (N, E, S or W, FeedW wide). Terminal 1 is the feed — the via on ViaFrom, or the stub's end — and terminal 2 is the pad centre. Leave terminal 2 open for a test point that is not in use, or continue it to a connector.

The pad loads the line with its capacitance to the nearest plane and the via's inductance, and the two resonate. The model is an estimate: the pad's capacitance to the nearest plane on each side, as a disc over a plane, with the dielectrics between combined in series; the via's inductance over its length, with the barrel's capacitance to each plane it passes. Every inner conductor counts as a plane under the pad unless ClearLayers names it. Messages gives the values and the resonance once per run. Rows that do not apply to the chosen Feed are greyed out in the parameter dialog: FeedW through a via, and ViaFrom, Drill, InnerPadD and AntipadD for a side-fed pad.

Unused pads on the via. Board CAD usually keeps a pad on every conductor a via passes, joined to nothing, and each adds capacitance across its antipad. Set InnerPadD to their diameter and the model counts them (and the layout draws them) on every conductor between ViaFrom and PadLayer that ClearLayers does not name; AntipadD is the clearance round the via in each plane (empty: the technology's). Messages gives their share separately. Removing unused pads at manufacture removes it.

Cut-outs. ClearLayers names the conductors whose plane gets a round cut-out ClearD across under the pad; the parameter dialog lists the technology's conductors to tick. Where the nearest plane is cut, the pad faces it over the ring outside the hole and the next plane through the hole, so its capacitance falls as ClearD grows and settles once the hole is a little wider than the pad. ClearD = 0, or one no wider than the via's AntipadD, cuts nothing: those planes are modelled as ordinary planes, and Messages says so. In a plane the via passes, its barrel sees the larger of ClearD and AntipadD. Cut-outs are not drawn as shapes: a ground pour drawn by Update Layout or Draw Ground Pour cuts them, as it cuts a via's antipad. On a board whose planes are drawn artwork, right-click the placed pad and choose Cut Clearances into Planes.

An EM port at the centre. With Centre = Port the layout carries an EM port at the pad's centre, an internal port to ground numbered PortNum (empty: the next free number). An EM setup of the board picks it up from inside the placed part — in 3D as a sheet from the pad to the nearest plane with metal there, through any cut-out — so the pad can be solved with and without each cut-out before a board is built. See Ports a component carries.

GSG Probe Pad (GSGPAD)

A ground-signal-ground probe pad and the microstrip line leaving it, for an RF probe landing on a die or a board. The signal pad sits between two ground pads at Pitch — centre to centre, the probe's own pitch — each ground pad holding NVia vias to the plane in a row along it, and a line W wide and L long leaves the signal pad. Terminal 1 is where the probe's signal tip lands, the middle of the signal pad; terminal 2 is the line's far end. Put the measurement port on terminal 1. In the layout the probe approaches from the side away from the line.

The model is MLIN: half the signal pad, PadW wide and PadL/2 long, then the line, cascaded. The ground pads are ideal ground at the probe's tip, which is where a calibrated probe puts its reference; their vias are drawn but are not part of the circuit. It is a microstrip, never a coplanar line: the ground pads stop at the signal pad and do not run along the line. The vias are a Via to Ground's, landing on the plane under the line — on a die, backside vias — with the technology's drill and pad; a ground pad grows longer when its row of vias needs the room. NVia = 0 draws no vias, for ground pads grounded some other way.

W is set to the 50 Ω width when the part is placed on a technology. Pitch, PadW and PadL are in µm and are the probe's, so no technology changes them.
