Dividers and couplers

Each part here is one RF topology, placed as one component and stated by what you specify rather than by its geometry: the port impedance and the centre frequency, a coupler's coupling, a delay line's electrical length or a pad's attenuation. There are twelve: the Wilkinson divider, the branch-line and rat-race hybrids, the Gysel, Bagley polygon and tee dividers, the coupled-line coupler, the interdigitated coupler, the coupled-line balun, the Schiffman phase shifter, the delay line, and the resistive attenuator and splitter. circuitRF works out the lines on the workspace technology's substrate, the same way every time, and the layout draws exactly the pieces the circuit model simulates, so the schematic, the layout, LVS and EM all read the same few numbers. The parameters panel shows what the specs come out to — the widths, gaps and lengths, and a ring's radius — as values you read, not type. A lumped part the topology needs, such as a Wilkinson divider's isolation resistor, is not inside the component: it is an ordinary part on two of its pins, with its own land pattern, so it reaches the layout, LVS and the bill of materials as itself.

Sites. A lumped part a component needs has a site: a pair of its pins (a series site) or one pin to ground (a shunt site), filled by an ordinary part — on a board an SMT resistor, inductor or capacitor, on a die a TFR, MIMCAP or SPIRAL, and for a ground or a crossover a VIAGND, a bond wire or an AIRBRIDGE. The parameters panel lists every site with the value the design wants there and, where the part sets it, the span between its pins. Place Site Parts, on the component's context menu and under that list, puts a part of that value on each empty site, wired to its pins, as one step you can undo; it leaves a jumper (a bond wire or air bridge) and a balun's load for you. The Gysel divider's resistors, the coupled-line rat-race's vias and the coupled-line coupler's capacitors and jumpers have no site: place them by hand, as on any pin. Where the span is a parameter (Gap on MWPD, MCBL, MLAD and MRPAD, and on MBLC and MRRC when lumped), it is a length by default; give the component a Footprint, in the same spelling a resistor's takes, and the span becomes that land's instead, for the run, the layout and LVS alike. The part on the site must then have the same footprint: Update Layout from Schematic reports one that does not fit, and LVS names the site and both footprints. A coupled array's sites are to ground and have no span, so its Footprint only chooses its capacitors' land.

Lumped realisations. The Wilkinson divider, the two hybrids and the balun also come lumped: Realization = Lumped replaces each quarter-wave line by the inductors and capacitors that equal it at F, and every one of them, with the divider's resistor, is a site. The component's own copper is then only the short lines that join the sites, one Z0 line width wide, laid out so that every series site's two pins face each other across Gap (or the Footprint's span) and every part to ground stands on a pin of its own, named G…. Its terminals are the ports and the sites' pins, and the parameters panel lists every value. Choose it below about a tenth of the frequency where a quarter wave fits comfortably, or on a die, where a quarter wave is too long to draw: it is a few millimetres across where the lines would be centimetres. The values are exact at F with the joining lines left out; the lines are in the model, and on 20 mil RO4350B at 500 MHz, with 0402 spans, they leave every port's match and the isolation below −15 dB and the split within 0.5 dB of 3 dB. The branch-line, with four parts at each corner, is the most affected: −19.7 dB, and 2.86 and 3.38 dB. Its band is narrower than the lines': like them it is exact at F only, and its lumped elements depart from the lines' behaviour away from it. On a die, put a TFR, SPIRAL or MIMCAP on each site; the parts are not sized for the values for you yet.

Wilkinson Divider (MWPD)

An in-phase two-way power divider on microstrip. Power into terminal 1 divides equally between terminals 2 and 3, which leave in phase, matched and isolated from each other at the centre frequency F; K makes the split unequal and N adds sections for a wider band (below). It works the other way round as a combiner. R2 and R3 are the ends of the two arms beside outputs 2 and 3: place a resistor of 2·Z0 on them (dropped on the symbol's R2–R3 pins it needs no wire) and give it a land pattern. Design ▸ Update Layout from Schematic lays the resistor across the gap the ring closes on and puts each port on its own pin.

How it works. The input meets two arms, each a line of √2·Z0 a quarter of a wavelength long at F. A quarter-wave line turns the Z0 load at its far end into (√2·Z0)²/Z0 = 2·Z0 at the input, and the two arms side by side are Z0 again, so the input is matched. Driven from an output, the divider is easiest seen as two halves: with both outputs driven alike nothing flows through the resistor, and with them driven opposite the resistor's midpoint is a virtual ground, so each output sees half of it, Z0, through its arm — matched, and the power that would have crossed to the other output is spent in the resistor instead. At F the ideal divider has S11 = S22 = S33 = 0, S23 = 0 and |S21| = |S31| = 1/√2, −3.01 dB.

What circuitRF derives. Every number below is recomputed from Z0 and F on the technology's substrate, by the one function the model and the layout share:

  • the arm width, for √2·Z0, and the port line's width, for Z0, each from the microstrip line model's own impedance at F;
  • the quarter wavelength, c₀ / (4·F·√εeff), with εeff the arm's effective permittivity at F, including dispersion;
  • the ring. The arms leave an input tee, turn 180° and come back facing each other across Gap; each ends in an output tee whose branch is terminal 2 or 3. A quarter wave is measured between the tees' reference planes: the straight run on the input tee plus the bend's effective length, π·(R − 0.2·W), which fixes the bend's centre-line radius R;
  • the isolation resistance, 2·Z0, which the readout states. The resistor itself is yours.

Each terminal is one port-line width of Z0 line beyond its tee, so a port lands on a line rather than in a junction's fringing field.

The model is the MTEE and MCURVE parts the layout draws, stamped together and reduced to the five terminals. It therefore has their limits, and says so in Messages: MTEE's junction formulas are calibrated on alumina (εr 9.9) and on W/h from 0.5 to 2, and MCURVE's length rule is stated for bend radii of 3 to 7 widths. A ring at low frequency is larger than that, where the bend's correction is a few per cent of a length that is right to first order. A specification the substrate cannot build is refused by name: an impedance no width reaches, or a quarter wave too short to make a ring (too high an F, or too wide a Gap).

The divider is narrowband. Its match and isolation are exact at F only. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) the circuit model keeps |S11| and |S23| below −20 dB from about 2.0 to 2.8 GHz.

In EM. Name the resistor as a component port. The ring joins R2 to R3 the long way round, so the resistor's two pads lie on one piece of copper and its port closes a loop (A part across a loop). At RF that is an ordinary port, and closing it with the 100 Ω gives the isolation. The run warns that the port's 0 Hz row reads the ring's copper. The Dividers and Couplers example runs it on Planar MoM, EMerge and Palace.

Gap is the span of the resistor's pins, 1.35 mm for an 0402 at nominal density. Change it with the land pattern, or let the land pattern set it:

Parameter What it is
Footprint Optional. The resistor's land, smt:<case>[@density] or a cell, as a resistor's own Footprint is spelt. When set, every resistor site's span is that land's (where a line meets each pad's outer edge) and Gap is not used; the resistors on R2–R3 (and R2_k–R3_k) must have the same footprint (Sites).

Unequal split: K

K sets how the power divides: port 3 takes K² times what port 2 takes. K = 1 is the equal split; K = 1.4142 sends twice the power to port 3, 3.01 dB more; a K below 1 favours port 2 the same way.

How it works. The resistor must carry nothing when the divider is driven from terminal 1, so the two arms' far ends have to sit at the same voltage while delivering different powers. A power P into a resistance R is V²/R, so the two ends are made to look like different resistances: K·Z0 at port 2's end and Z0/K at port 3's. With P3 = K²·P2 the two voltages are then equal. Each arm is a quarter wave that turns its end's resistance into what the input needs to divide in that ratio, which gives arms of Z0·√(K(1 + K²)) to port 2 and Z0·√((1 + K²)/K³) to port 3, and each output then needs a quarter-wave transformer of Z0·√K or Z0/√K to bring its end back to Z0. Driven from the outputs, the isolation resistor that matches them and spends the cross-coupled power is Z0·(K + 1/K), 2·Z0 at K = 1.

What circuitRF derives on top of the equal split: the two arms' impedances and widths, the two transformers', each line's quarter wave, and the resistor. The two arms have different effective permittivities, so their quarter waves are different lengths; both curve on one radius, so the input tee's two straight runs differ instead and the resistor's gap sits a little off the input's line. Each transformer is the branch of its output tee, and the terminal is at its end.

Limits. Port 2's arm grows as K^1.5: on 20 mil RO4350B, K = 2 already asks for a 158 Ω line, and K = 4 for 412 Ω, which no width reaches; a split the board cannot draw is refused (device.wilkinson.split-unrealisable), naming the line. The unequal split is one section only. At K = 1 the transformers would be Z0 lines that change nothing, so the equal split leaves them out; a K just off 1 puts them in, so its outputs are a quarter wave further from the junction, 90° later.

Broadband: N sections

N = 2 to 7 cascades that many quarter-wave sections, each with its own isolation resistor, to divide over a band rather than at one frequency. Band is the band's upper edge over its lower, f2/f1, centred on F (2, an octave, by default). The part grows two terminals per section: resistor 1 goes on R2–R3 at the outputs as before, and resistor k on R2_k–R3_k, counted from the outputs inward; the readout lists every section and every resistor's value. Dropped on the symbol's pins, each resistor needs no wire.

How it works. Driven from terminal 1, both halves carry the same signal and no resistor carries current, so each half is simply a chain of quarter waves from 2·Z0 (half of the input) down to Z0 (an output). One quarter wave can match that at one frequency; N of them can keep the reflection small across a band. circuitRF makes it equal-ripple (Chebyshev) from f1 = 2F/(1 + Band) to f2 = 2F·Band/(1 + Band), with the section impedances symmetric about √2·Z0 (z_k·z_(N+1−k) = 2·Z0²), so its reflection is exactly zero at N frequencies inside the band. Driven from the outputs in antiphase, the input junction is a virtual ground and each resistor's midpoint is ground too, so each half is a shorted chain of the same sections with half of each resistor across it at every junction. The resistors are solved so that this half is exactly matched at those same N frequencies (N equations, N resistors); there every port is matched and the outputs are isolated. The one-section divider is the N = 1 case of the same rule.

For an octave, the sections and resistors, from the outputs inward, in units of Z0:

N Sections Resistors
1 1.4142 2
2 1.2196, 1.6399 4.8428, 1.9539
3 1.1130, 1.4142, 1.7970 10.468, 3.9009, 1.9410
4 1.0591, 1.2572, 1.5908, 1.8883 21.380, 6.5989, 3.6670, 1.9667
7 1.0089, 1.0568, 1.1863, 1.4142, 1.6859, 1.8924, 1.9823 161.45, 29.964, 11.677, 7.0555, 5.2838, 3.8258, 2.0029

Two and three sections are solved by a bisection on the first section's impedance; four to seven by the same two conditions for any N, solved together (a Gauss–Newton step on the transformer's reflection, Newton's method on the resistors), started from a 10:1 band where the solution is easy to find and carried to the band asked for in 5 % steps. The general solve gives the two- and three-section numbers too, to eleven places. The resistor at the outputs grows quickly with N: at an octave it is 21·Z0 for four sections and 161·Z0 for seven, where it does little, and the one nearest the input stays near 2·Z0.

Layout. The ring is the section next to the input. Each further section is a pair of straight lines run on from the ring's output tees, one each side of the gap's centre line, with a tee at every junction whose short branch reaches the gap's edge, so every resistor lands across the gap at its own junction as the first one does on the ring.

Limits. The pair of lines run side by side about Gap apart, and the model treats them as separate lines: their coupling to each other is not in it. EM includes it; on the example board the EM isolation follows the model's to a few dB, so there it is small, but a narrow Gap on a thick substrate couples more. The tees at the junctions are MTEE's model, with its limits. N sets the number of terminals, so it must be a plain number, not an expression or a swept variable; above 7, a Band not above 1 (or under 1.1 with four or more sections, where the resistors' equations become dependent), or a K other than 1 with more than one section is refused by name.

On the example board, the two-section divider keeps |S11| below −20 dB from 1.31 to 3.22 GHz and |S23| from 1.31 to 3.36 GHz, a 2.5:1 band, where one section does from 1.98 to 2.85 GHz and from 1.92 to 2.77 GHz, 1.4:1. It pays for it with a quarter wave more line, 0.09 dB more loss at F, and a shallower null at F itself (|S11| −26 dB rather than −48).

Corners: Corner

Corner says how the ring turns. Curve, the default, is the 180° bends described above. Miter and Square draw the ring as a rectangle instead: each arm rises from the input tee, turns 90°, runs across, turns again and comes back to its output tee. A Miter corner is an MMITER at its usual chamfer, the Douville–James optimum for the arm's W/h; a Square corner is an MBEND with no chamfer.

What circuitRF derives. A corner has an electrical length of its own, and circuitRF takes it from the corner's own model at F on the substrate (its phase between two lines of the arm's impedance) and shortens the straight runs by it, so each arm is still a quarter wave at F between the tees' reference planes, corners included. On the example board at 2.4 GHz a mitred corner stands for 0.57 mm of the arm; left in, the two corners would make each arm 6 % long and lift |S11| at F from −52 dB to −30 dB. The rectangle is as tall as the curved ring, so its two arms stay a ring's width apart: the model does not include coupling between them, and a flatter rectangle would run them side by side. Both arms span one width between the tees; with K ≠ 1 the arm that needs more line takes up the difference in its rise and fall, so the gap stays on the input's line. Every K and N works with either corner, and the parameters panel shows each arm's runs and what one corner stands for.

When to choose it. Choose a corner when the layout wants a rectilinear outline: to sit on a placement grid, to run lines alongside it, or to pack several parts close together. Prefer Miter: on the example board the mitred divider is matched and isolated at F as well as the curved one (|S11| −52 dB against −48, |S23| −36 dB for both), while square corners reflect, from the excess capacitance an unchamfered corner carries, and hold |S11| at −29 dB. Use Square where the board's rules or its fabrication call for edges on the grid alone.

Lumped: Realization

Realization = Lumped makes the lumped divider: each √2·Z0 arm becomes a network that equals the quarter wave at F, and Arm chooses which:

  • Pi, the default: a series inductor L = √2·Z0/ω between two capacitors to ground of C = 1/(ω·√2·Z0), with ω = 2π·F. The two arms' capacitors at the input add, so the input has one of 2·C on G1 and each output one of C, on G2 and G3. The arms' inductors go across L1a–L1b and L2a–L2b;
  • Tee: two series inductors of the same L about one capacitor to ground of the same C: L1a–L1b and L2a–L2b on the arm to 2 with its capacitor on G1, L3a–L3b and L4a–L4b on the arm to 3 with its capacitor on G2.

The isolation resistor, 2·Z0, stays on R2–R3, across the gap between the outputs' junctions. A π uses two inductors where a T uses four, so it is the usual choice where inductors are the lossy parts. The lumped divider is the equal split in one section: K other than 1 or N other than 1 with Lumped is refused.

Parameter What it is
Realization Distributed (the default): the quarter-wave ring above. Lumped: the lumped divider; the terminals become 1, 2, 3, R2, R3, the inductors' pins and the G pins.
Arm With Lumped: Pi or Tee, what stands in for each arm.

More than two ways

Wilkinson's paper divides N ways at once: N quarter-wave arms of √N·Z0 from the input, and a resistor of Z0 from each arm's end to one common point. MWPD does not draw it, because for three ways or more it cannot be drawn on one layer. Every output's line has to leave the divider for its port, so count the board's edge as one more node: the input, the resistors' common point and the edge are each joined to every one of the outputs. With three outputs that is the three-by-three "utility" graph, which no drawing in a plane makes without a crossing; a real N-way divider needs an air bridge, a second layer or a resistor laid over a line. The two-way divider's version of that graph is planar, which is why its ring closes across one gap.

The planar answer is a tree of two-way dividers: 4 ways is three MWPDs, and the Dividers and Couplers example draws one. Three equal ways is an unequal MWPD with K = 1.4142, which sends a third to port 2 and two thirds to port 3, followed by an equal MWPD on port 3, and on port 2 a line as long as that divider if the three outputs must be in phase.

The nets of an instance line, in this order. Not interchangeable: terminal 1 is the input and 2 and 3 the two outputs, alike by symmetry when K = 1. R2 and R3 are the arms' ends beside outputs 2 and 3, the gap the isolation resistor goes across: put a resistor of 2·Z0 (Z0·(K + 1/K) for an unequal split) on R2-R3. With N sections the terminals are 3 + 2·N: R2_k and R3_k, k = 2 … N, are the ends of resistor k, counted from the outputs, and the Properties readout gives every resistor's value. With Realization = Lumped the terminals are the lumped divider's: 1, 2 and 3, R2-R3 for the resistor, each arm's inductor across L1a-L1b and L2a-L2b (π) or L1a … L4b (T), and a capacitor to ground on each G pin.

Branch-Line Hybrid (MBLC)

A 3 dB quadrature (90°) hybrid on microstrip, in one to four sections. Two through lines, 1–2 and 4–3, are joined by quarter-wave shunt arms. Power into terminal 1 divides equally between terminal 2 (through) and terminal 3 (coupled), which leave a quarter period apart, 3 behind 2; terminal 4 is isolated and every terminal is matched at the centre frequency F. The coupler is symmetric, so any terminal can be the input, with the other three taking the same roles around the ring.

How it works. The coupler is a mirror image of itself across the line midway between the two through lines, so a drive at terminal 1 can be split into an even half (1 and 4 driven alike) and an odd half (driven opposite). In the even half the midline is an open circuit, in the odd half a short, and each shunt arm becomes an eighth-wave stub, open or shorted, on a single through line. Each half is then a two-port that can be solved on its own, and the four S-parameters are the halves' sums and differences: S11 and S41 come from the two reflections, S21 and S31 from the two transmissions. With one section — series arms of Z0/√2 and shunt arms of Z0, all a quarter wave long — both halves are matched at F, and they transmit with equal magnitude and a quarter period apart: S11 = S41 = 0, S21 = −j/√2 and S31 = −1/√2, so |S21| = |S31| = −3.01 dB with 3 lagging 2 by 90°.

Two sections, three shunt arms, give a wider band. Normalise each arm's admittance to the ports' (t for the series arms, a for the two outer shunt arms, b for the middle one): the halves are matched and the fourth terminal isolated when b = 2·a·t² / (1 + a²), and the split is 3 dB when b / t² = 1/√2. circuitRF keeps the series arms at Z0 (t = 1), which gives a = √2 − 1 and b = 1/√2: outer shunt arms of (1 + √2)·Z0 and a middle one of √2·Z0, 120.7 Ω and 70.7 Ω in a 50 Ω system. At F it is matched, isolated and split 3 dB, the through port now half a period behind the input and 3 again a quarter period behind 2.

Three and four sections keep the series arms at Z0 too, and solve the shunt arms from the same two conditions at F. At F each half is a chain of quarter waves with an eighth-wave open (or shorted) stub at every junction, and its ABCD matrix has A = D; the half is matched when B = C, and the split is 3 dB in quadrature when |B| = 1/√2. Three sections, four shunt arms a, b, b, a, have a closed form: b = √(1 − 1/√2) and a = √2·b·(√(1 + 1/√2) − 1), shunt arms of 4.26·Z0 and 1.85·Z0, 213 Ω and 92.4 Ω in a 50 Ω system. Four sections, five shunt arms, leave one value free once both conditions hold; circuitRF sets the middle arm so the match is flat at F as well as exact, which gives shunt arms of 7.40·Z0, 2.55·Z0 and 1.99·Z0 from the outside in.

The outer arms are the limit. Each section added widens the band and raises the outer arms' impedance. 213 Ω on 20 mil RO4350B is a line 1.3 µm wide, which the line model accepts and no board draws, and whose conductor loss takes 1 dB of the split; on 60 mil PTFE (εr 2.2) it is 70 µm, and there the three-section coupler is matched and isolated to −43 dB at F. Four sections' 7.40·Z0 is 370 Ω in a 50 Ω system, outside the line model on both boards and refused by name; in a 35 Ω system on the PTFE board it is 259 Ω and 11 µm wide.

What circuitRF derives from Z0, F and N on the technology's substrate, by the one function the model and the layout share:

  • each arm's width, from the microstrip line model's own impedance at F, and the ports' Z0 width;
  • each arm's length, a quarter of a guide wavelength at F, c₀ / (4·F·√εeff) with εeff the arm's own effective permittivity at F, including dispersion, measured between the reference planes of the two MTEEs it joins: a through arm from half the branch's width, a shunt arm from half the wider through arm's;
  • with two sections, one span for all three shunt arms, since both through lines are straight: each shunt arm takes the mean of the arms' quarter waves, about 1.5 % from its own on the example board.

Each terminal is one port-line width of Z0 line beyond its tee, in line with the through line, and each tee carries one port-line width of its shunt arm before the arm's own line begins, so the circuit model includes the junction. The parameters panel shows each arm's width, impedance and length.

The model is the MTEE and MLIN parts the layout draws, stamped together and reduced to the four terminals, with their limits, which it reports in Messages: MTEE's junction formulas are calibrated on alumina (εr 9.9), on W/h from 0.5 to 2 and on a branch of 25 to 100 Ω, and the two-section coupler's 120.7 Ω outer arms are outside the last. The junctions' own reactance moves the best match a little below F: 2.36 GHz for F = 2.4 GHz on the example board, where |S11| is still −30 dB at F. A specification the substrate cannot build is refused by name: an impedance no width reaches, an arm too short to leave each tee its stub (a high F), or N other than 1 to 4.

The coupler is narrowband. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) the circuit model keeps |S11| and |S41| below −20 dB from 2.24 to 2.49 GHz with one section, and from 2.08 to 2.64 GHz with two. The Dividers and Couplers example runs the one-section coupler on Planar MoM, EMerge and Palace.

Lumped. Realization = Lumped makes the lumped coupler (Vogel): each arm a π at F, a series inductor of the arm's impedance over ω between two capacitors to ground. The series arms' inductors, Z0/(√2·ω), go across L1a–L1b (1 to 2) and L3a–L3b (4 to 3), the shunt arms', Z0/ω, across L2a–L2b (2 to 3) and L4a–L4b (1 to 4), and each corner's two capacitors add to one of (1 + √2)/(ω·Z0) on G1 to G4. One section only.

Rat-Race Hybrid (MRRC)

A 3 dB 180° hybrid on microstrip: a ring with four terminals on it. Terminal 1 is the sum (Σ) port and terminal 4 the difference (Δ) port; 2 and 3 are the outputs. Power into 1 divides equally between 2 and 3, in phase, and 4 is isolated; power into 4 divides equally between 2 and 3, half a period apart, and 1 is isolated. Driven at 2 and 3 together it works the other way round, delivering their sum at 1 and their difference at 4. 2 and 3 are isolated from each other.

How it works. The ring is a line of √2·Z0, one and a half guide wavelengths round, with the terminals in the order 2, 1, 3, 4 spaced a quarter, a quarter, a quarter and three quarters of a wavelength apart. Seen from terminal 1, each output is a quarter wave away one way round the ring and five quarters the other, so the two paths arrive in phase and add; terminal 4 is half a wave away one way and a whole wave the other, so they cancel. From terminal 4 the two outputs are a quarter wave and three quarters away by their shorter paths, so they leave half a period apart. Each quarter-wave path of √2·Z0 turns a Z0 load into 2·Z0, and two of them side by side are Z0 again, so every terminal is matched. The same result follows from splitting the ring into even and odd halves about its line of symmetry, as for the branch-line hybrid. At F the ideal hybrid has S21 = S31 = −j/√2, S24 = −S34 = j/√2, and S11, S44, S41 and S23 zero.

What circuitRF derives from Z0 and F on the technology's substrate, by the one function the model and the layout share:

  • the ring's width, for √2·Z0, and the ports' Z0 width, from the microstrip line model's own impedance at F;
  • the quarter wavelength, c₀ / (4·F·√εeff) with the ring's effective permittivity at F, and every spacing measured between the reference planes of the MTEEs on the ring;
  • the ring's shape. Its pieces turn only in quarter turns, so the terminals cannot sit 60° apart on a circle: the ring is two straight runs joined by two 180° bends, terminals 2, 1 and 3 on one run with their lines leaving the same way and terminal 4 on the other. Closing it with one tee on one run against three on the other fixes the bends: π·(R − 0.2·W) = λg/4 − W0, with W the ring's width, W0 the ports' and R the bends' centre-line radius.

Each terminal is one port-line width of Z0 line beyond its tee. The parameters panel shows the widths, the quarter wavelength and the bends' radius.

Corners. Corner = Miter or Square turns each end of the ring on two 90° corners, an MMITER at its usual chamfer or an MBEND with none, with a straight side between them, so the ring is a rectangle (as the divider's). Each end is still λg/4 − W0 of line: the two corners at their own electrical length at F, taken from the corner's model, plus the side, which is that much shorter. On the example board |S11|, |S44|, |S41| and |S23| stay below −49 dB at F with mitred corners (−49 to −51 dB with the bends) and below −42 dB with square ones. Choose it for the same reasons as the divider's, Miter first.

Folded: Meander. Meander = k, an odd number of turns, folds the three-quarter-wave arm inside the ring, a compact rat-race in the line of Eccleston and Ong's, who shortened the arms with artificial lines, and He and Wang's, who meandered them. The three quarter-wave arms make a C: 2 to 1 along the top, 1 to 3 a U-turn, 3 to 4 along the bottom. The long arm closes the C from the inside: a half-turn back in from terminal 4's tee, a meander of k turns between the top and bottom runs, laid by the same function as a delay line's, and a half-turn out to terminal 2's tee. Its half-turns' own electrical length at F comes out of the meander, so it is still three quarters of a wavelength, and every turn of it has the same radius, which puts its legs as far from one another as from the runs. The ring is no taller and about a quarter wave narrower: on the example board the copper, feeds included, is 29.87 × 13.57 mm with one turn, against 53.11 × 14.24 mm for the curved ring, 54 % of its area, and at F the outputs are the curved ring's to 0.002 dB, the match and the isolation below −49 dB in both, and the in-phase and antiphase outputs within 0.02° of 0° and 180°, about 0.2° closer than the curved ring's: the folded arm is sized by the line's causal phase at F, the curved ring by its effective permittivity alone. The folded legs are separate lines in the model, uncoupled to each other and to the runs beside them; the turns are curves only, so Corner must be Curve. Meander = 0, the default, is the ring above, unchanged.

Coupled-line: Form. Form = CoupledLine makes the compact rat-race of March (10.1109/TMTT.1968.1126693). The three-quarter-wave arm becomes a coupled pair a quarter wave long with two diagonal far ends grounded: at F that is a 270° line of 2·Ze·Zo/(Ze − Zo), so with that set to √2·Z0 it takes the long arm's place at a third of its length, and the ring is a square of the three quarter-wave arms and the section. Coupling (10 dB by default) sets the section's other degree of freedom, March's own being 3 dB. The section lies along the bottom: terminal 4's tee on one strip's near end, terminal 2's on the other's far end, and the two grounded ends are terminals G2 and G4, G2 inside the ring beside terminal 2's tee and G4 below terminal 4. Place a via to ground (VIAGND) on each, as on the balun's. The arms go around the other three sides with a corner each, a quarter-turn curve or an MMITER or MBEND by Corner, counted at its own electrical length.

Not every board builds it. Whatever the coupling, the section needs 1/Zo − 1/Ze = √2/Z0, 0.028 S at 50 Ω. At the narrowest gap the coupled-line model covers (S/h = 0.1) edge coupling reaches about 0.033 S on 100 µm GaAs, 0.028 S on 25 mil alumina and 0.022 S on 20 mil RO4350B: so a 50 Ω ring builds on GaAs (a 10 dB section of 227 µm strips 11 µm apart at 10 GHz), and on that board from about 65 Ω up; otherwise the part says so by name, giving the admittance it needs. At F on GaAs, with ideal vias, the match is −52 dB at Σ and −40 dB at Δ, the isolation −49 and −41 dB, and the outputs within 1.5° of in phase and of 180°. Meander must be 0 with this form; Realization = Lumped takes precedence.

The model is the MTEE, MLIN and MCURVE parts the layout draws, stamped together and reduced to the four terminals, with their limits, which it reports in Messages: MTEE's junction formulas are calibrated on alumina (εr 9.9) and on W/h from 0.5 to 2, and MCURVE's length rule is stated for bend radii of 3 to 7 widths, a smaller ring than most. A specification the substrate cannot build is refused by name: an impedance no width reaches, or a quarter wave too short to leave the bends a radius of one ring width (too high an F).

The hybrid is narrowband. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) the circuit model keeps |S11|, |S44|, |S41| and |S23| below −20 dB from 2.04 to 2.71 GHz. The Dividers and Couplers example runs it on Planar MoM, EMerge and Palace.

Lumped. Realization = Lumped makes the lumped hybrid. The three quarter-wave spacings, 2 to 1, 1 to 3 and 3 to 4, are each a π at F: an inductor of √2·Z0/ω across L1a–L1b, L2a–L2b and L3a–L3b. The three-quarter-wave spacing, 4 to 2, is its high-pass dual, which turns the phase the other way, +90° where the line turns −270°: a capacitor of 1/(ω·√2·Z0) across C1a–C1b. At 1 and at 3 two π ends meet, and their capacitors add to one of √2/(ω·Z0) on G1 and G3. At 2 and at 4 a π's capacitor meets the high-pass section's inductor to ground; the two resonate at F, an open circuit there, and are left out. Corner does not apply.

Gysel Divider (MGPD)

An in-phase two-way power divider on microstrip whose isolation resistors go to ground. Power into terminal 1 divides equally between terminals 2 and 3, in phase, matched and isolated from each other at the centre frequency F. R2 and R3 are the isolation nodes beside outputs 2 and 3: the resistors are not part of the part. Place a resistor of Z0 from each to a via to ground (VIAGND); Design ▸ Update Layout from Schematic puts each resistor on its pin and its via beside the resistor's far pad. Because each resistor has one end grounded, it can be as large as the power it has to take, sit on its own heat sink, or be a termination off the board on a connector: that is what the divider is for, combining amplifiers whose imbalance would overheat a Wilkinson's floating resistor.

How it works. The ring runs 1, 2, R2, R3, 3 and back to 1: a quarter wave of √2·Z0 from the input to each output, a quarter wave of Z0 from each output to its isolation node, and a half wave of Z0/√2 between the two isolation nodes. Split it into halves about the line through terminal 1 and the half wave's middle. Driven alike, the outputs see an open at the half wave's middle; a quarter wave from it each isolation node is a short, so its resistor carries nothing, and a quarter wave further the isolation arm is an open at the output. Each output then sees only its input arm, which turns the input's 2·Z0 half into Z0. Driven opposite, terminal 1 and the half wave's middle are virtual grounds: the input arm and the half line are shorted quarter waves, opens at the output and at the isolation node, and the output sees its resistor through the isolation arm, Z0²/R, which is Z0 when R = Z0. Matched in both halves, every terminal is matched and the outputs are isolated at F. The half wave's impedance does not enter at F: it sets the band, and a lower one widens it (on ideal lines |S11|, |S22| and |S23| stay under −20 dB over ±9 % of F with Z0, ±11 % with Z0/√2, ±12 % with Z0/2); circuitRF takes Z0/√2, whose width stays within about twice the port line's.

What circuitRF derives from Z0 and F on the technology's substrate, by the one function the model and the layout share: the three lines' widths, from the microstrip line model's own impedance at F, and their quarter waves in each line's own effective permittivity at F, every spacing measured between the reference planes of the tees on the ring; and the ring's shape. As the rat-race's, it is two straight runs joined by two 180° bends: 2, 1 and 3 on the upper run with their lines leaving upward, R2 and R3 on the lower run with theirs downward and the half wave between them; each isolation arm goes round a bend, and the lower run carries the difference in length as a short line at each end. Corner = Miter or Square turns each end on two 90° corners instead, as the divider's, the corners' own electrical length taken out of the side between them. Each terminal is one port-line width of Z0 line beyond its tee; at R2 and R3 that line is matched by the Z0 resistor at its end, so it changes nothing.

The model is the MTEE, MLIN and MCURVE (or MMITER and MBEND) parts the layout draws, stamped together and reduced to the five terminals, with their limits, which it reports in Messages. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) with 50 Ω on R2 and R3, |S11|, |S22| and |S23| are −50, −59 and −52 dB at F, the split −3.15 dB each, and all three stay under −20 dB from 2.11 to 2.65 GHz, with any Corner. A specification the substrate cannot build is refused by name: an impedance no width reaches, or a quarter wave too short to leave the bends a radius of one line width (too high an F).

Bagley Polygon Divider (MBPD)

A lossless N-way divider on microstrip with no resistors, for an odd number of outputs, 3 by default. Power into terminal 1 divides equally among terminals 2 to N + 1, which N sets: the pin count follows it. The outputs alternate in phase: 2, 4, 6 … leave a quarter period behind the input and 3, 5 … half a period from those. Only the input is matched; the outputs see each other and are not isolated, so it suits feeding equal loads, such as an antenna array's elements, where a sign can be taken up by the element's orientation or a half-wave line.

How it works. The outputs are the corners of a polygon whose sides are half-wave lines of Z0, and the input feeds the middle of the one side that closes it, a quarter wave from the first corner and from the last. A half-wave line repeats the voltage at one end at the other, inverted, so every corner has the same amplitude and neighbouring corners are opposite; N must be odd so the two ways round from the input agree at every corner. Equal voltages into equal loads take equal power. The input arms then only have to match: the corners' currents add up to N·V/(2·Z0) at the first and last corners, which a quarter wave of Z_a turns into Z_a²·N/(4·Z0) at the input, Z0 when Z_a = 2·Z0/√N: 57.7 Ω for three ways in a 50 Ω system. The sides' impedance does not enter at F; Z0 gives the widest input match at three ways (on ideal lines, |S11| under −20 dB over ±17 % of F).

What circuitRF derives from Z0, F and N on the technology's substrate, by the one function the model and the layout share: the input arms' and the sides' widths and quarter waves at F, every spacing measured between the reference planes of the tees on the ring, and the ring's shape. It is laid out as the Gysel's: the input on the upper run between its two nearest corners, the far corners on the lower run, and the side that crosses from one run to the other round each bend, so the runs come out nearly equal. Corner turns the ends on 90° corners, as the divider's does.

The model is the MTEE, MLIN and MCURVE (or corner) parts the layout draws, stamped together and reduced to the terminals. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) the three-way divider's |S11| is −46 dB at F and stays under −20 dB from 1.95 to 2.73 GHz, and each output takes −4.9 dB; five ways with square corners, −38 dB at F and each output −7.0 dB. A specification the substrate cannot build is refused by name, as is an even N or one above 9.

Tee Divider (MTPD)

The simplest divider: one tee junction whose two arms are quarter-wave transformers to the outputs. Power into terminal 1 divides between terminals 2 and 3, in phase, port 3 taking K² times what port 2 takes. Only the input is matched; the outputs see each other and are not isolated, as nothing dissipates what one reflects. Choose it where the outputs are well matched loads and isolation does not matter, or as the junction of a corporate feed.

How it works. At the junction the two arms are in parallel, and each must look like the resistance that takes its share of the power: Z0·(1 + K²) towards port 2 and Z0·(1 + K²)/K² towards port 3, which together are Z0. A quarter wave of Z_t turns the output's Z0 into Z_t²/Z0, so the transformers are Z0·√(1 + K²) to port 2 and Z0·√(1 + K²)/K to port 3: √2·Z0 each for the equal split.

What circuitRF derives from Z0, F and K on the technology's substrate: each transformer's width and its quarter wave at F, from the junction's reference plane to its terminal. The part is that one MTEE: the input on its branch, one port-line width of Z0 line from the junction, and the transformers its two through arms.

The model is MTEE's, with its limits. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) |S11| is −29 dB at F, the junction's own reactance moving the best match a little low, and stays under −20 dB from 1.85 to 2.67 GHz; the outputs see each other at −6 dB.

Coupled-Line Coupler (MCLC)

A single-section backward-wave directional coupler on microstrip: two edge-coupled strips a quarter wavelength long at F. Power into terminal 1 goes on to the through port, terminal 2, and a fraction of it, Coupling dB down, appears at the coupled port, terminal 3, beside the input; the isolated port, terminal 4, ideally gets none. The coupled wave leaves 90° ahead of the through wave. Its pins are MCLIN's, so the part is an MCLIN whose W, S and L are chosen for you.

How it works. A symmetric pair carries two modes: the even mode, both strips at one voltage, and the odd mode, the strips at opposite voltages, each a line of its own impedance, Ze and Zo. With Ze·Zo = Z0² every port is matched at every frequency, and at the quarter wave the coupled voltage is c = (Ze − Zo)/(Ze + Zo). So a coupling of C dB, with c = 10^(−C/20), asks for Ze = Z0·√((1 + c)/(1 − c)) and Zo = Z0·√((1 − c)/(1 + c)).

What circuitRF derives. The strip width and gap whose even and odd impedances at F are those two, found from the coupled-line model itself (the Kirschning–Jansen equations MCLIN uses), and the length, c₀ / (4·F·√εeff) with εeff the mean of the two modes' effective permittivities at F. The search covers the model's published range, W/h and S/h from 0.1 to 10: a coupling that would need a narrower gap, or a wider one, is refused by name.

Microstrip's limit is directivity. The odd mode has more of its field in the air and travels faster than the even mode, so the strips cannot be a quarter wave for both. Coupling and match hold at F; the isolated port picks up the difference. On the example board (20 mil RO4350B, 2.4 GHz) the circuit model gives about 11 dB of directivity at 10 dB coupling and under 5 dB at 20 dB. Tight coupling needs narrow gaps there: 10 dB needs 115 µm, 8 dB 65 µm.

In EM the coupling lives in that narrow gap, and the mesh has to resolve it: the Dividers and Couplers example runs the 10 dB coupler on Planar MoM with its edge mesh on (within 0.25 dB of the model at F) and on EMerge and Palace with refined meshes; their coarsest presets read the coupling several dB too strong.

Options: sections, broadside, tandem, compensation

Each option is off by default, and with all of them off the coupler is the single section above, to the last digit. They are one at a time: the coupler refuses two together by name.

Option What it builds Choose it for Source
Sections = 3, 5, 7 or 9, with Band That many quarter-wave pairs in a row, the middle one tightest, so the coupling ripples equally about Coupling over Band (f2/f1, centred on F) A flat coupling over an octave or more Cristal and Young, 10.1109/TMTT.1965.1126050
Broadside = 1 One pair on two conductors, one over the other: BCLIN's stripline pair on a stack with a ground above and below, MBCLIN's otherwise Tight coupling, 3 dB included, that no edge gap reaches the models of BCLIN and MBCLIN
Tandem = 1 Two identical couplers, each of the weaker coupling that adds up to Coupling, joined so their couplings add A broadband 3 dB hybrid from two buildable couplers of 8.34 dB Shelton, Wolfe and Van Wagoner, Microwaves, April 1965 (no DOI); Carpenter, 10.1109/GMTT.1971.1122878
Compensation = Capacitive The pair re-synthesised so a capacitor across each coupled end equalises the two modes at F; the readout gives its value Directivity, with a part on 1–3 and on 2–4 Dydyk, 10.1109/MWSYM.1990.99647, 10.1109/22.769332
Compensation = Inductive A short narrow line in series at each of the four ends, and a pair a little shorter than a quarter wave Directivity with no extra parts Phromloungsri, Chongcheawchamnan and Robertson, 10.1109/TMTT.2006.881026
Compensation = Wiggly The facing edges drawn as a saw-tooth, so the odd mode's path is longer by the ratio of the two modes' speeds Directivity with no extra parts or length Podell, 10.1109/GMTT.1970.1122761

Sections. With Ze·Zo = Z0² in every section, a coupler of TEM lines is matched and isolated at every frequency, and its coupled wave is the reflection of the chain of even-mode impedances. circuitRF designs that chain for an equal ripple of the coupling over the band, the optimum Cristal and Young tabulate, then finds each section's pair as for one section. The sections are drawn in a row about one gap centre line; where they meet, the strips step in width, and the step itself is not modelled. On 20 mil RO4350B a 15 dB coupler of three sections, designed for ±0.03 dB over 2:1, keeps its coupling within 0.23 dB from 1.6 to 3.2 GHz, where one section varies by 1.3 dB. The tightest section is the middle one, so a tight coupling over a wide band soon needs a gap the board cannot build.

Broadside. The two strips are on the signal layer and the conductor directly below it, so the coupling no longer lives in a narrow gap: on a four-layer board with 2 mil between the top two copper layers, 3 dB needs the strips about 0.12 mm apart sideways. The width and the sideways offset are found from the pair's own field solution, which costs a few seconds; terminals 3 and 4 are on the lower layer. A technology with no second signal layer next to the signal layer is refused by name, and so is a coupling tighter than the strips reach one over the other.

Tandem. Two couplers of voltage coupling c1 in tandem couple 2·c1·√(1 − c1²): two of 8.34 dB make 3 dB. They are drawn one above the other, joined around both ends by lines of equal length, so the coupled wave arrives at the through port 2 and at the coupled port 3, here at the far end, in quadrature. Each joining line encloses one port's lead, which no flat layout avoids, so each is broken where that lead crosses it: J1–J2 and J3–J4 are the crossovers, and each takes a jumper — a bond wire, an air bridge or an underpass — placed as an ordinary part, as the interdigitated coupler's fingers are joined. Terminals 1 and 3 have straight leads as long, at F, as the bent leads of 2 and 4. On 20 mil RO4350B a 3 dB tandem splits within 1 dB of even from 1.7 to 2.8 GHz with its outputs 90° apart to within a degree.

Compensation. Microstrip's odd mode is faster than its even mode, which is what limits a plain coupler's directivity (11 dB at 10 dB coupling on the example board). Each form makes the two modes equal electrical lengths at F again:

  • Capacitive: a capacitor C across the gap at each end loads only the odd mode. The pair is a quarter wave in the even mode, and C = (cos θo − cos θe) / (2·ω·Zo·sin θo), with θ each mode's electrical length, makes the odd mode one too; the pair is re-synthesised so that loaded mode still gives the coupling. Place a capacitor of the readout's value on 1–3 and on 2–4. On the example board, 0.17 pF lifts the directivity at 10 dB from 11 dB to over 45 dB.
  • Inductive: a series reactance X at each of the four ends adds more electrical length to the odd mode than to the even one; X = Ze·cot θe = Zo·cot θo fixes a pair a little shorter than a quarter wave. Each X is a short line twice Z0 in impedance, whose own shunt capacitance is what keeps this short of ideal: 24 dB of directivity on the example board.
  • Wiggly: the facing edges are a saw-tooth about one strip width long per tooth, as deep as makes their path √(εeff,e/εeff,o) times the length. The circuit model is only approximate: it is the pair's own modes with the odd mode's length multiplied by that factor, the correction Podell describes; the teeth also change the odd mode's capacitance, which it does not see, and it says so in Messages. EM is the judge of a wiggly coupler.

Interdigitated Coupler (MIDC)

A four-finger interdigitated quadrature coupler on microstrip — the Lange coupler, unfolded. Four quarter-wave strips lie side by side; alternate strips are joined at both ends into two conductors, so each conductor couples to the other across three gaps instead of one and reaches couplings a single pair cannot. Terminals 1 to 4 are as MCLC's: 1 the input and 2 the through port on the top finger, 3 the coupled port and 4 the isolated port on the bottom finger. J1 to J4 are the inner fingers' ends: the joins are not part of the part. Place a jumper from each terminal k to Jk — on a board, a bond wire across the finger between — so the layout, LVS and EM see it as the part it is. Each k–Jk pair is a series site.

How it works (Ou's equations). With only neighbouring fingers coupled, every finger has a capacitance to ground and a mutual capacitance to each neighbour, and both can be read off one pair of adjacent fingers: an outer finger's ground share is the pair's even-mode admittance 1/Ze, the mutual is half the difference of the odd and even admittances, and a finger between two others keeps less of the ground share because its neighbours screen it. Adding the fingers of each conductor, with each conductor at one potential, gives the coupler's own modes: Ze,N = Ze(Ze + Zo)/(Ze + (N − 1)·Zo) and Zo,N = Zo(Ze + Zo)/(Zo + (N − 1)·Ze), with N = 4 here, and a coupling (N − 1)(R² − 1)/((N − 1)(R² + 1) + 2R) with R = Ze/Zo. circuitRF inverts that for Coupling and Ze,N·Zo,N = Z0², then finds the adjacent pair's W and S exactly as MCLC does. The length is a quarter wave in the pair's mean εeff.

The model is the pair's own modes, MCLIN's, put through Ou's equations, with each finger carrying its own share of each mode: an ideal jumper on each Jk gives Ou's two-conductor coupler exactly, a real jumper carries its finger's current, and a missing one is a different circuit, which still solves and couples less. Ou's equations are a TEM picture; the even and odd permittivities are the adjacent pair's, and fingers further apart than neighbours are not coupled.

What a board can build. A 3 dB coupler needs tight gaps. On 20 mil RO4350B at 2.4 GHz it needs fingers 138 µm wide and 69 µm apart, under common board rules of 75 to 100 µm; 3.5 dB needs 86 µm and 4 dB 105 µm. The part opens at 4 dB for that reason, splitting about −2.4 dB and −4.2 dB in quadrature. A thinner laminate, or a process with finer gaps, reaches 3 dB.

Six or eight fingers. Fingers = 6 or 8 builds that many, with Ou's equations for that N (10.1109/TMTT.1975.1128534): more fingers couple more across a wider gap. Each further pair of inner fingers adds four landings, so the part has 2·N terminals: J(4m + k) joins terminal k's conductor (k = 1 to 4), by a jumper from terminal k or from the landing beside it. The finger pair's own impedance rises with N, about N/2 times Z0 at weak coupling, so on a board six or eight fingers suit a low Z0 or a thin substrate: at 50 Ω their fingers are narrower than the coupled-line model's range on 20 mil RO4350B and are refused, while a 25 Ω six-finger coupler builds 3 dB there.

Coupled-Line Balun (MCBL)

A compensated coupled-line balun on microstrip — the Marchand balun in planar form. It turns the unbalanced signal on terminal 1 into two outputs of equal amplitude and opposite phase on terminals 2 and 3. Two quarter-wave coupled sections lie in a row: the input strip runs along both, across a line of length Gap between them, to an open end, and each section's other strip is a balanced output at the middle and grounded at its outer end. G2 and G3 are those outer ends: the grounds are not part of the part. Place a via to ground (VIAGND) on each.

How it works. At the quarter wave a coupled section's open-circuit impedances reduce to two terms: between the ends of one strip, (Ze + Zo)/2, and between the far ends of the two strips, (Ze − Zo)/2. Solving the two sections with the open end and the grounds gives output voltages exactly equal and opposite whatever the loads, so long as they are alike, and an input impedance 2·(Ze·Zo)² / (ZL·(Ze − Zo)²) with ZL on each output. With lines of √(Ze·Zo) = Z0, matching that to Z0 needs each section to couple c = 1/√(1 + 2·ZL/Z0); circuitRF finds the pair for it as MCLC does.

ZL is the load on each output, half the balanced load. The match fixes the difference of the two mode admittances, 1/Zo − 1/Ze = √(2/(ZL·Z0)), at whatever impedance level, and edge coupling at a buildable gap only reaches it for high loads. On 20 mil RO4350B at 2.4 GHz, 50 Ω on each output needs −4.8 dB sections, a gap under the model's 0.1·h, and is refused; 200 Ω on each output needs −9.5 dB and a 102 µm gap, which is what the part opens at.

Microstrip's limit is the phase. The output voltages are exactly opposite only for TEM lines. In microstrip the odd mode runs faster than the even, neither section is a quarter wave for both, and on the example board the outputs come out about 16° short of 180°, with their amplitudes within 0.2 dB. A longer Gap moves the match off F.

G2 and G3 are shunt sites for a via each, and outputs 2 and 3 face each other across Gap, the site of the balanced load:

Parameter What it is
Footprint Optional. The land of a two-pad part across outputs 2 and 3, smt:<case>[@density] or a cell. When set, the joining line is that land's span (where a line meets each pad's outer edge) and Gap is not used; the part across 2–3 must have the same footprint (Sites).

In EM the Dividers and Couplers example runs a balun with vias on G2 and G3 on EMerge and Palace. The Planar solver refuses it: its via-current kernel is validated to a tenth of a wavelength between vias, and the two grounds sit a balun's length apart.

Lumped. Realization = Lumped makes the balun a lattice of two inductors and two capacitors (Bakalski et al.): an inductor from 1 to 2 (L1a–L1b) with a capacitor to ground at 2 (G2), and a capacitor from 1 to 3 (C1a–C1b) with an inductor to ground at 3 (G3). Each inductor is X/ω and each capacitor 1/(ω·X), with X = √(2·Z0·ZL): at F the outputs are equal and exactly opposite for any equal loads, 90° either side of the input, and with ZL on each the input is Z0. Unlike the coupled lines, a lattice reaches any ZL, 50 Ω on each output included, and its outputs are 180° apart on any board. Gap is then each series site's span.

Parameter What it is
Realization Distributed (the default): the coupled-line balun above. Lumped: the lattice.

Schiffman Phase Shifter (MSPS)

A differential phase shifter on microstrip: two separate paths whose phases differ by Phase at F and stay close to it over a band. Terminals 1 and 2 are the ends of a C-section, a coupled pair a quarter wave long whose far ends are joined by a short strap; terminals 3 and 4 are the ends of a reference line. Either end of each path can be its input.

How it works (Schiffman). With Ze·Zo = Z0² the C-section is matched at every frequency, and its phase φ follows tan(φ/2) = tan θ/√ρ, with ρ = Ze/Zo and θ its electrical length: 180° at the quarter wave, changing fastest there. The reference line, k quarter waves long with k = (Phase + 180°)/90°, changes at a steady rate, so the difference kθ − φ is Phase at F and, for the right ρ, ripples equally about it over the band f2/f1 = Band. circuitRF finds that ρ, then the pair for it as for the coupled-line coupler; 90° over 1.5:1 needs ρ = 2.40 (a 7.7 dB pair, ±0.6°), over 2:1 ρ = 2.73 (±2.7°), and 90° needs ρ = 2.25 however narrow the band.

What circuitRF derives. The pair's width, gap and length — the length is where the C-section's own model, strap included, is exactly 180° at F, so the difference is exactly Phase there on the board — and the reference line's width and length. Reference lays the reference line straight (Straight, terminal 4 at the far end) or folded back beneath itself so terminal 4 is beside terminal 3, on a 180° curve (Curve) or two corners (Miter, Square); every turn counts at its own electrical length. Meander folds it once as a delay line's meander is laid, its pitch chosen so each leg is the C-section's length: the reference lies under the section as one block, all four terminals in a column on its left edge, and its phase holds through the turn (the difference is the straight reference's to 0.001° on the example board). The parameters panel shows ρ, the pair, the reference line and the ripple.

Microstrip's limit. Schiffman's design is for TEM lines. In microstrip the odd mode is faster, so the C-section is not a quarter wave in both modes and its match suffers: on 20 mil RO4350B at 2.4 GHz its return loss at F is about 12 dB where TEM lines would be perfect, and the strap adds a little inductance. The phase difference holds to about a degree over 1.5:1 there. A tight ρ also needs a narrow gap: 90° needs at least 8.3 dB of coupling.

Delay Line (MDLY)

A length of microstrip stated by its electrical length: Theta at F, laid straight, round one corner, or folded into a meander to fit a smaller space. Use it as a delay, a phase shifter's reference arm, or wherever a line must be a given phase long at a given frequency. Terminal 1 is where the run starts and terminal 2 where it ends; the line is reciprocal, so either may be the input.

What circuitRF derives from Z0, F and Theta on the technology's substrate:

  • the width, for Z0, from the microstrip line model's own impedance at F;
  • Theta as a length of that line, by its phase constant at F: its effective permittivity's and the phase its loss comes with, as the line model stamps it;
  • the layout, by Style:
    • Straight: one line of that length;
    • Corner: two equal legs and one 90° corner, a curve of three widths' radius (Corner = Curve), a mitred corner (Miter) or a square one (Square);
    • Meander: Turns + 1 equal parallel legs joined by Turns 180° turns, Pitch apart centre to centre (0: six widths, so a half-turn's radius is three widths), stacked to the left of the run's heading from terminal 1 (Side = 1) or to its right (−1). A turn is a half-turn of radius Pitch/2, or two corners and the line between them. An odd number of turns ends heading back the way the run started.

The length holds through the corners. Every corner or turn has its own phase at F, taken from its own model, and the legs are shortened by it, so S21 is −Theta at F in every style: on the example board within 0.04° for straight, cornered and meandered runs of 90° to 360°. The parameters panel shows the width, Theta as a straight length, the copper's length along its centre line, its extent and each run in order.

Legs that couple. Legs close together couple, which slows the run and moves its phase. With Coupled = 0, the default, they are separate lines in the model and the run says so in Messages when they are under three widths apart edge to edge. Coupled = 1 puts the legs into the model as one section of N coupled lines, every leg coupled to every other, over the same copper. On the example board a 360° meander of three half-turns at 2.4 GHz is then 1.3° off −Theta with its legs ten widths apart, 3.2° at four and 6.1° at two; the 1.3° that remains far apart is the coupled-line section's static permittivity against the single line's dispersive one, and the phase the single line's loss comes with, which the coupled-line section leaves out. The turns are never coupled to one another.

The model is the MLIN, MCURVE, MMITER or MBEND parts the layout draws (and with Coupled the coupled-line section), stamped together and reduced to the two terminals, with their limits, which it reports in Messages: MCURVE's length rule is stated for radii of 3 to 7 widths, so a meander's half-turns sit inside it at pitches of six to fourteen widths. A run too short for the turns asked of it, a pitch no wider than the line, or a turn count that is not a whole number is refused by name.

Resistive Attenuator and Splitter (MRPAD)

A matched resistive pad: an attenuator of Attenuation dB between terminals 1 and 2, or a three-port splitter, Z0 at every port. It has no lines of its own: every resistor is a site, and the part is the short Z0-wide lines that join them, so each resistor is an ordinary part with its own land, as the lumped dividers' are. Form chooses the network; with K = 10^(Attenuation/20):

Form Resistors
Pi Z0·(K² − 1)/(2·K) across R1a–R1b, and Z0·(K + 1)/(K − 1) from each of 1 and 2 to ground.
T Z0·(K − 1)/(K + 1) across each of R1a–R1b and R2a–R2b, and 2·Z0·K/(K² − 1) from 3 to ground.
BridgedT Z0 across each of R1a–R1b and R2a–R2b, Z0·(K − 1) across R3a–R3b, which bridges them from 1 to 2, and Z0/(K − 1) from 3 to ground.
Wye Z0/3 from each of 1, 2 and 3 to the middle, across R1a–R1b, R2a–R2b and R3a–R3b.
Delta Z0 between each two of 1, 2 and 3, across R1a–R1b (1–2), R2a–R2b (2–3) and R3a–R3b (3–1).

Terminal 3 is a splitter's third port. On a T or BridgedT it is the middle node, where the shunt resistor goes to ground; brought out, it is where a T pad's shunt arm can be returned elsewhere, and the bridged-T and the two splitters share one set of terminals. The π's shunt resistors sit on 1 and 2 themselves.

The values are the textbook matched pads: with each resistor ideal and the joining lines left out, each form is matched at every port and loses exactly Attenuation dB (an attenuator) or 20·log10 2 = 6.02 dB between any two ports (a splitter, whose loss is fixed by matching all three; Attenuation does not apply). A bridged-T keeps its two series resistors at Z0 for every loss and changes only the other two, which is why it is the form to tune. The joining lines are in the model, and add their own small phase and reactance as the frequency rises.

Parameter What it is

Planar filters

A filter here is one component stated by its geometry: the widths, lengths and gaps you or a filter synthesis chose. Unlike the dividers and couplers above, nothing is derived from a specification, so the part draws and simulates exactly the numbers it holds, on whichever technology it is placed. The layout draws the pieces the circuit model simulates, and LVS compares every stored dimension and name. There are three, each one family of filters:

  • the coupled-resonator filter (MCRC): edge-coupled, zig-zag, hairpin, open-loop, cross-coupled and ring bandpass filters, and bandstop and spurline filters;
  • the microstrip ladder (MLAD): an ordered list of lines, gaps, tapers, stubs and lumped parts, which holds the stepped-impedance, stub and end-coupled filters, matchers, transformers and LC ladders;
  • the coupled array (MCLA): interdigital, combline and pseudo-interdigital filters.

A ladder's and an array's vias, capacitors and lumped parts are sites, which Place Site Parts fills as it does a divider's.

Coupled-Resonator Filter (MCRC)

One part for every coupled-resonator microstrip filter: N resonators, each coupled to the next across a gap, between an input on terminal 1 and an output on terminal 2. Five names choose what it is.

  • Shape, how each resonator is laid out:
    • Straight, the parallel-coupled (edge-coupled) filter: each half-wave resonator lies in two halves, the first beside the resonator before it and the second beside the one after;
    • ZigZag, the same, each resonator folded 90° at its middle, alternately right and left, so the filter runs in steps instead of a long diagonal;
    • Hairpin, each resonator folded into a U whose arms are Sa apart, the U's alternately inverted, neighbouring arms coupled;
    • OpenLoop, square loops each opened by Gap in the middle of one side. Arrangement = Inline sets them in a row, opened alternately at the top and the bottom; Cross sets four in a square, loops 1 and 4 cross-coupled across Sx, as in Hong and Lancaster's quasi-elliptic four-pole filter, with a transmission zero either side of the passband;
    • Ring, one ring L round, fed across S1 and S2 from a short line on either side.
  • Profile: Uniform, or SIR, a stepped-impedance resonator (Makimoto and Yamashita) whose centre is Wc wide over Uc of its length, for Straight, ZigZag and Hairpin. A narrow centre shortens the resonator and moves its first spurious response up; a SIR hairpin is the miniature hairpin. The hairpins are staggered so their wide ends face.
  • Feed: Coupled, a strip beside the first and the last resonator, or Tapped, a line joined to each, Tap along it from its midpoint (further out couples more strongly). A tapped filter has no S1 or S(N+1).
  • Form: Bandpass; Bandstop, resonators beside a through line, alternately above and below, each coupled over its first half (ZigZag: the other half folded away) or one arm (Hairpin), notching where it is half a wavelength; Spurline, each resonator a spur cut into a through line 2·W + S wide by an L-shaped slot S wide (Bates), notching where the spur is a quarter wavelength in the coupled pair's odd mode.
Parameter Meaning
N Resonators. A Ring is one; the Cross loops are four.
W, W1, W2, … Each resonator's width, and the feed strip's beside it; Wk gives resonator k its own. Neighbours coupled side by side take one width.
L, L1, L2, … Each resonator's centre-line length, open end to open end, about half a guided wavelength; Lk gives resonator k its own. Corners count along the centre line. A loop's is its perimeter less Gap, a ring's its circumference.
S1 … S(N+1) Sk is resonator k's gap to the resonator or feed before it; S(N+1) the output feed's. A bandstop's Sk is resonator k's gap to the through line, a spurline's its slot.
S Every gap not given its own Sk, as W and L are for Wk and Lk: switched to four cross-coupled loops, a part takes S5 from it.
Sa, Gap, Sx The hairpin's arm gap, the loop's opening, the cross-coupling gap.
Tap A tapped feed's distance from the end resonator's midpoint.
Wc, Uc A SIR's centre width and its share of the length.
Coupling Pairs (the default) or Full: what the circuit couples, below.

Building it. Every coupled length is an MCLIN pair, every other run an MLIN, every fold a mitred MMITER corner, a ring two MCURVEs, a tap an MTEE, a ring's feed and a loop's opening an MGAP, and every free end an open end. Each strip couples to the neighbour it lies against, which is what the textbook design methods design with; a hairpin's own two arms, strips further over and the corners are not coupled in the circuit, and an EM run of the artwork has them. A neighbour longer than the next couples over the shorter one's end; its extra length is a plain line. A combination the part cannot build is refused by name: a bandstop of straight resonators (coupled along their whole half wave they do not notch), a stepped profile on a loop, a tap that lands on a corner, and, with Coupling = Pairs, neighbours of unequal width coupled side by side.

Coupling. Pairs, the default, couples each strip to the neighbour it lies against as an MCLIN pair, which has one width. Full places every coupled region as one section of the N-line model (MCLINN), with every strip its own width, so neighbours of unequal width build and each width can be the design's. For a hairpin it goes further: every arm that lies beside others over the same stretch is in one section, so a hairpin's own two arms couple, and so does every arm beyond its neighbour; for aligned hairpins that is one section of every arm and both feed strips. The artwork is the same either way. With the arms well apart the two agree closely (on the default board a hairpin filter's band moves by 0.5 % with the arms four widths apart); with the arms close, Full has the arms' own coupling that Pairs leaves out (4.4 % higher and 27 % narrower with the arms half a width apart). Full still leaves out what is not side by side: the corners, a cross-coupled square's diagonal, a longer neighbour's overhang. The N-line model is quasi-static and solves each cross-section once, a few seconds for eight strips.

Designs. The part does not synthesise. Textbook designs placed in it land where they were designed: on 20 mil RO4350B a three-resonator 2.4 GHz filter 10 % wide with 0.5 dB ripple, from Cohn's parallel-coupled method, comes within 1 % of its centre and 6 % of its ripple bandwidth as Straight, ZigZag and Hairpin, and an open-loop design from Hong and Lancaster's coupling coefficients within 1 % and 5 %. The default values are the Straight design. On a 100 µm GaAs or silicon process the part takes the substrate from the technology like any line.

Microstrip Ladder (MLAD)

One through line from terminal 1 to terminal 2, built from an ordered list of sections: series lines, gaps and tapers, shunt stubs at junctions along it (open, shorted, or ending on a radial or butterfly stub), and sites for lumped parts. One part holds stepped-impedance and stub lowpass filters (the elliptic kind included), radial-stub and butterfly lowpass filters, shorted-stub bandpass and highpass filters, quarter-wave stub bandstop filters, end-coupled bandpass filters, DC blocks, single- and double-stub matchers, multi-section quarter-wave transformers, and semi-lumped and lumped LC ladders. Sections is the list; Z0 is the impedance of the lines the ladder is fed by, F the frequency the readout states each section at, and Gap the span a series site leaves for its part.

The parts and the grounds are not part of the part. A shorted stub ends on a terminal of its own, and a site's part goes on terminals of its own: G1, G2, … in the list's order, one per shorted stub arm, one per shunt site and two per series site. Place a via to ground (VIAGND) on each shorted stub's terminal, and the site's R, L or C on its terminals: across the two of a series site, or from a shunt site's one to ground. Place Site Parts does both, with the values the list states. Design ▸ Update Layout from Schematic places each via beside its stub's end and lays a series site's part across the copper's two ends.

The list. Sections are separated by ; and each is kind(field=value, …), in the order they lie from terminal 1:

Section Fields What it is
line(W=…, L=…) width, length A series line.
gap(S=…) gap A series end-to-end gap, between two ends of the width the ladder has there.
taper(W1=…, W2=…, L=…) the two widths, length A series linear taper.
stub(W=…, L=…, end=…, side=…) width, length; end open or short; side up, down or both A shunt stub at a junction, L from the through line's edge to its end. end=open and side=up unless stated. both is a stub on each side, W and L each.
stub(W=…, L=…, end=radial, Ro=…, angle=…) as above; the sector's radius from its apex and its angle in degrees (60 unless stated) A stub whose end is a radial stub (MRADIAL): a feed W wide and L long, then a sector whose narrow end is W, fanning away from the line. end=butterfly is two sectors either side of the feed's end.
site(role=…, value=…, type=…, side=…) R, L or C; its value (3.3pF, 12nH, 4.7kOhm); series or shunt; for a shunt site up or down A place for a lumped part. Series (unless stated): the copper stops Gap short and the part goes across. Shunt: a square pad off the line, the part from its end to ground.

A length is a number in metres, or a number with a length unit written straight after it: 1.1mm, 250um, 40mil, 0.5cm. A bare m means milli in circuitRF, not metres, so 1m is refused. Names may be in any case, and spaces are ignored. The width "there" is the Z0 line's at the ladder's ends, and past a line or taper it is that section's. A wrong section is refused with its number and its text, for example Ladder: section 2 (stub(W=1mm)): stub needs L.

What it is made of. Each section is the part it would be on its own: a line is MLIN, a gap MGAP, a taper MTAPER, a one-sided stub an MTEE whose branch is the stub, a two-sided stub an MCROSS, and a radial end MRADIAL. A site is copper only: a series site's two ends, Gap apart (or a Footprint's land, which the ladder takes as MWPD does), and a shunt site's pad, a square of the line's width on a tee. Where a series site has no copper beside it (at either end, after a gap, or next to another series site) it gets a pad of its own there, so an LC ladder of sites alone is a row of pads with the parts between and beside them. An open stub's end includes the field that fringes past it, as the extra length Kirschning, Jansen and Koster give for an open end. So a stub that is to be θ long at F is written that length less its open end's extension, which the readout states. The terminals sit exactly at the first section's start and the last section's end, so a matcher or a transformer ends on its own load.

The readout lists every section at F on the technology's substrate: a line's or a stub's impedance and electrical length (an open stub's end extension beside it, and a radial end's reactance), a taper's impedance at each end and its length, a gap's series and end capacitances, and each site's part. Then it lists the sites with their terminals, values and spans, which is what Place Site Parts fills them with.

Limits. The step between two widths is not modelled, and neither is coupling between neighbouring stubs. The pads a lumped ladder stands on are in the model, and their own inductance and capacitance are not in a lumped design's values: on 20 mil RO4350B they lower a 1 GHz LC lowpass's cutoff about 5 %, and a 200 MHz one's about 1 %. MTEE's and MCROSS's junction formulas are calibrated on alumina (εr 9.9) and say so in Messages on any other board. A closed-form design places each stub at a point, while the model includes each junction's own reactance. That moves a filter's frequencies by an amount set by the junction. The two cases below where it matters most are a stub wider than the line it stands on, and a double-stub matcher on a load of low conductance.

Examples on 20 mil RO4350B, each worked out from its closed form, with lengths rounded to the micrometre:

  • Stepped-impedance lowpass (Butterworth, N = 6, cutoff 2.5 GHz). Each shunt capacitor g is a 15 Ω line of βl = g·15/50, and each series inductor a 120 Ω line of βl = g·50/120, at the cutoff. The −3 dB point is 2.38 GHz: short lines only approximate the inductors and capacitors. line(W=5.482mm, L=1.637mm); line(W=0.114mm, L=7.026mm); line(W=5.482mm, L=6.108mm); line(W=0.114mm, L=9.597mm); line(W=5.482mm, L=4.471mm); line(W=0.114mm, L=2.572mm)
  • Open-stub lowpass (Richards and Kuroda, Butterworth N = 3, cutoff 2.4 GHz). Every section is λ/8 at the cutoff. The series stubs become shunt stubs by Kuroda's identity: open stubs of 100, 25 and 100 Ω joined by 100 Ω lines. The 25 Ω stub is drawn as two 50 Ω arms. The −3 dB point is 2.35 GHz. stub(W=0.223mm, L=9.517mm); line(W=0.223mm, L=9.661mm); stub(W=1.058mm, L=9.015mm, side=both); line(W=0.223mm, L=9.661mm); stub(W=0.223mm, L=9.517mm)
  • Elliptic kind: a stepped-impedance lowpass with stubs. The prototype's shunt capacitor becomes an open stub that is λ/4 at the wanted zero, here 3.12 GHz, and has the capacitor's admittance at the 2.4 GHz cutoff. The zero falls at 3.21 GHz: the stub is wider than the 100 Ω line it stands on, and the junction shortens it. line(W=0.223mm, L=6.150mm); stub(W=0.635mm, L=14.274mm); line(W=0.223mm, L=6.150mm)
  • Shorted-stub bandpass (Matthaei, Butterworth N = 3, centred on 2.4 GHz). Quarter-wave shorted stubs of π·Z0·Δ/(4·g) are joined by quarter-wave 50 Ω lines, each stub two arms of twice that. With Δ = 1 the −3 dB band is 1.67 to 3.05 GHz. It has six via terminals, G1 to G6. stub(W=0.432mm, L=19.037mm, end=short, side=both); line(W=1.058mm, L=18.460mm); stub(W=1.554mm, L=18.170mm, end=short, side=both); line(W=1.058mm, L=18.460mm); stub(W=0.432mm, L=19.037mm, end=short, side=both)
  • Shorted-stub highpass: the same design made wide (Δ = 1.6 about 4.8 GHz). The shorted stubs stop DC: it is below −28 dB at 0.48 GHz and passes from about 2.9 GHz to 6.7 GHz, where the stubs near a half wave. stub(W=0.699mm, L=9.360mm, end=short); line(W=1.058mm, L=9.211mm); stub(W=0.699mm, L=9.360mm, end=short, side=both); line(W=1.058mm, L=9.211mm); stub(W=0.699mm, L=9.360mm, end=short, side=down)
  • Quarter-wave stub bandstop (Butterworth N = 3 over Δ = 0.5 about 2.4 GHz). Open stubs of 4·Z0/(π·g·Δ) are λ/4 at the centre, joined by quarter-wave 50 Ω lines. The notch is at 2.415 GHz, −81 dB. stub(W=0.087mm, L=19.459mm); line(W=1.058mm, L=18.460mm); stub(W=0.681mm, L=18.573mm); line(W=1.058mm, L=18.460mm); stub(W=0.087mm, L=19.459mm)
  • End-coupled bandpass (Cohn, Butterworth N = 3, 3 % wide at 10 GHz, on 25 mil alumina, where gaps reach the outer couplings). Each J-inverter is a gap whose series capacitance gives it, and each half-wave resonator is shortened for the inverters and for the gaps' end capacitance. The passband is centred on 10.004 GHz. gap(S=0.028mm); line(W=0.618mm, L=5.098mm); gap(S=0.576mm); line(W=0.618mm, L=5.293mm); gap(S=0.576mm); line(W=0.618mm, L=5.098mm); gap(S=0.028mm)
  • DC block: one gap. Terminals 1 and 2 are separate copper. gap(S=0.1mm)
  • Single-stub matcher, 60 − j80 Ω to 50 Ω at 2 GHz: a shorted 50 Ω stub, 0.110 λ from the load. |S11| is −52 dB. stub(W=1.058mm, L=8.418mm, end=short); line(W=1.058mm, L=9.787mm)
  • Double-stub matcher, 40 − j30 Ω to 50 Ω at 2 GHz: two open 70 Ω stubs λ/8 apart, the second at the load. Of the two solutions, this one's stubs change least with length. |S11| is −39 dB. stub(W=0.560mm, L=40.760mm); line(W=1.058mm, L=11.079mm); stub(W=0.560mm, L=35.318mm, side=down)
  • Quarter-wave transformer: three binomial sections from 50 to 100 Ω at 2.4 GHz, of 54.5, 70.7 and 91.7 Ω. |S11| is −78 dB. line(W=0.910mm, L=18.569mm); line(W=0.548mm, L=18.903mm); line(W=0.289mm, L=19.224mm)
  • Radial-stub lowpass: radial stubs on 0.5 mm feeds off 100 Ω lines, one up, a pair, one down. It passes 0.5 GHz with −0.2 dB and is below −30 dB from 3.5 to 5 GHz. line(W=1.1mm, L=3mm); stub(W=0.6mm, L=0.5mm, end=radial, Ro=6mm, angle=60); line(W=0.22mm, L=6mm); stub(W=0.6mm, L=0.5mm, end=radial, Ro=6mm, angle=60, side=both); line(W=0.22mm, L=6mm); stub(W=0.6mm, L=0.5mm, end=radial, Ro=6mm, angle=60, side=down); line(W=1.1mm, L=3mm)
  • Butterfly lowpass: a butterfly at the end of a 3 mm feed either side of a 100 Ω line, below −30 dB around 3 GHz. line(W=1.1mm, L=3mm); stub(W=0.6mm, L=3mm, end=butterfly, Ro=6mm); line(W=0.22mm, L=8mm); stub(W=0.6mm, L=3mm, end=butterfly, Ro=6mm, side=down); line(W=1.1mm, L=3mm)
  • Lumped LC lowpass (Butterworth N = 3, cutoff 200 MHz): series L of g·R0/ωc, shunt C of g/(R0·ωc), series L, all sites. Filled with the parts its sites state, its −3 dB point is 197.5 MHz. site(role=L, value=39.789nH); site(role=C, value=31.831pF, type=shunt); site(role=L, value=39.789nH)
  • DC block on a part: a series capacitor's site between two lines. line(W=1.1mm, L=5mm); site(role=C, value=10pF); line(W=1.1mm, L=5mm)

The nets of an instance line, in this order. How many there are is set by Sections; the table shows Sections = 2. Terminals 1 and 2 are the through line's ends, the first section at 1. G1, G2, … follow in the list's order: one per shorted stub arm (up before down), for a via to ground (VIAGND); one per shunt site, for its part to ground; and two per series site, for the part across them.
